entries.content:
I first learned of Ossabaw Island from Musa Mayer’s Night Studio (1988), a memoir of her life as Philip Guston’s daughter. At the time I was writing a short story about Guston and had grown fixated on his wife, Musa McKim, who’d given up painting for poetry. McKim’s time at Ossabaw in 1974 was one of the few occasions when she left his side, for a two-week residency to work on a manuscript. It offered a moment of revelation, or at least reversal. A letter Guston sent to McKim during her “vacation” is obsessive, spiraling, as if the magnetic center of his life had been temporarily removed: “Every minute my thoughts are with you—seeing you picked up at the DeSoto Hotel—by whom? Going to the Island—how?” he writes. “If only I knew—had seen Ossabaw—I would feel a little better—but as it is, I feel so lost, so alone without you.”

Ossabaw is a 26,000-acre heart-shaped barrier island off the coast of Georgia—a patchwork landscape of salt marshes and maritime forests, tidal creeks and interdune meadows, feral hogs and plovers, lofty cabbage palms and live oaks hung with portieres of Spanish moss. Its name, AW-suh-bah, from the Muscogee word for land of holly, is unhurried and airy, yet somehow also imbued with gravitas, more lavish than those of the other barrier islands: Cumberland, Sapelo. The Sea Islands, a three-hundred-mile archipelago that hugs the Eastern seaboard from South Carolina to Florida, have a long history of colonization, from the displacement of the Indigenous Guale and Mocama peoples by Spanish settlers in the sixteenth century to the British seizure of the territory around two hundred years later. The latter introduced a plantation economy centered on the cultivation of cotton, rice, and indigo, which required the labor of enslaved Africans; their appearance on Ossabaw was first recorded in 1763.

Following the Civil War, several freedmen were given tracts of land under Special Field Order No. 15—which Andrew Johnson soon overturned. Black sharecroppers continued to farm the island until a succession of violent hurricanes at the end of the nineteenth century caused many to flee. Several decades later, in 1924, the Torrey family, heir to the Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company and Wyandotte Chemicals Corporation fortunes, purchased the property after a catastrophic fire destroyed their storied Savannah plantation Greenwich Place, which allegedly rivaled the opulence of the Biltmore Estate in Asheville, North Carolina.

Off the Coast of Paradise: Artists and Ossabaw Island, 1960–Now—a marvelous exhibition at the Jepson Center at Telfair Museums in Savannah, Georgia—celebrates the island’s lasting, understudied imprint on American cultural history. Curated by Erin Dunn and Beryl Gilothwest, it presents a survey of more than thirty artists who participated in multidisciplinary retreats on Ossabaw, primarily in a pair of programs that ran from 1961 until 1982. Known as the Ossabaw Island Project (OIP) and Genesis, they had distinct yet complementary aims. The preservationist Eleanor “Sandy” Torrey West, the projects’ elegant patrician benefactor, founded OIP in 1961 with her second husband, Clifford Bateman West, a painter and educator, to provide time and space for established practitioners. They were given handsome accommodations in the Main House, a 20,000-square-foot pastel-pink Spanish Colonial Revival estate with fifteen bedrooms, or in its fairly plush auxiliary buildings. Genesis—OIP’s scrappier younger sibling, founded by the Wests nearly a decade later—had a more rough-and-tumble, DIY ethos, inviting early-career artists and graduate students to pursue a cooperative living model among the humble cabins of Middle Place Plantation, a former lumber camp without running water or electricity; each participant was responsible for five hours of chores and one meal per week. Ticks, chiggers, and bloodsucking conenoses were constant threats.

Ossabaw’s ventures often draw comparisons with fabled residencies in the northeast like Yaddo or MacDowell, but they were far more heterogeneous from the start. A list of visitors to Ossabaw reads like a Who’s Who of twentieth-century American cultural history, from writers like Ralph Ellison, Margaret Atwood, Annie Dillard, and Henri Cole to artists, composers, and architects including Sally Mann, Amy Sillman, Aaron Copland, Samuel Barber, Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown, Ellen Lanyon, Betty Tompkins, Arnold Blanch, and Doris Lee. But they also hosted scientists, historians, literary theorists, naturalists, religious leaders, philosophers, businesspeople, and anthropologists, including the linguist Roman Jakobson and Eugene Odum, remembered today as the “father of ecology.”

Many of the most celebrated cultural exports from OIP and Genesis—including Harry Bertoia’s bronze spill-casting technique, which culminated in his monumental Dulles International Airport commission, and Olive Ann Burns’s novel Cold Sassy Tree (1984)—are the direct or oblique results of conversations among individuals from different disciplines. Bertoia drew inspiration for his method, which involves heavily manipulating the surface of molten bronze, from “the constant battle of the elements” he witnessed on Ossabaw’s sand flats, as well as conversations with the biologist Colin Pittendrigh. Burns, who had worked primarily as a journalist, claims she never would have finished her manuscript without the encouragement of the literary theorist Menakhem Perry, a fellow OIP member, during her stay on the island.

Advertisement

Sandy West inherited the island from her parents in 1958 and soon felt a duty to share the place with artists and thinkers who might commune with and translate its unspoiled mystery. It was partially Sandy’s irrepressible belief in Ossabaw’s spiritual significance that convinced then-Governor Jimmy Carter, after a two-day visit in 1972, to sign the State of Georgia’s Heritage Preserve Act into law several years later. With his encouragement, she sold the island to the state in 1978 for half its estimated value of $16 million, forgoing private offers (including a substantial bid from Jacqueline and Aristotle Onassis) to ensure that it would be sanctified as Georgia’s first Heritage Preserve. Unlike Hilton Head, a nearby barrier island now considered the “Hamptons of the South,” Ossabaw remains almost entirely pristine and undeveloped, per Sandy’s wishes.

Today a vocabulary of enchantment still hangs over the island, mostly furnished by Sandy West, who called it “a tremendous catalyst” for creative experimentation and intellectual cross-pollination. Clifford West was similarly adamant that Ossabaw offer uninterrupted time and space for people who seemed patient, and perhaps suggestible, enough to thrive in the island’s resplendent seclusion. (Gilothwest, who currently serves as deputy director of research and exhibitions at the Calder Foundation, is the Wests’ grandson.) Both maintained a strong belief that creativity required freedom and inefficiency, and that these gifts should be given without any pressure to produce. Their goal was simple—to “get the right kind of people and then leave them completely alone”—and they understood that a direct encounter with the island would not necessarily yield immediate results. “You could come here and seem to be doing nothing at all,” Sandy once told a journalist, “but that’s when your imagination is really going into high gear.” This quiet faith in the pleasurable but fickle processes of creation was a principle from which the Wests never strayed.

Those who experienced Ossabaw in that era often speak of its sublimity and grandeur in superlatives that sound effusive to the point of panegyric, as if it were a land outside time. Miriam Schapiro wrote that Ossabaw was “nature at her romantic best”; press clippings refer to the island’s “wild beauty.” Yet residencies were hardly a holiday. “Ossabaw is not for everyone,” wrote the painter Jean Zaleski, “certainly not for the timid.” And if “this air supports miracles,” as the poet Carol Burdick wrote, it also bore extreme elemental volatility. Many visitors acknowledged the quasi-erotic thrill of nature’s indiscriminate rages: punishing storms overhead, venomous cottonmouths underfoot. Isolation from modern life meant that amenities such as hospitals and shops were not readily accessible. Signs on closet doors in the Main House read: “TIDES – SNAKES – GETTING LOST are ever present dangers. THIS IS IMPORTANT.”

Ascending the light-dappled stairs in the Jepson’s atrium, designed by Moshe Safdie, visitors to Off the Coast of Paradise confront a video montage that serves, in equal measure, as incantation and evocation: egrets scattered like specks of tow in a stretch of maritime forest; windtracked coastline flocked with sculptural driftwood; plain-faced tabby houses, charming and squat, set in a modest row. Inside, the exhibition opens with Marcy Hermansader’s Secrets of the Heart (1983), a magnetic, darkly brooding mixed-media arrangement of nested images that serve as portals into Ossabaw’s hidden depths.

Framed in a proscenium of clawlike branches is a primal scene of creation, a mesmerizing, whorling pastiche of the artist’s memories of a terrain that left a deep mark on her practice. Tantalizing forms emerge from the void: gently undulating ridges or waves recall early modern mappamundi; weeping-willow motifs quote early American mourning pictures. Slashes in the picture plane reveal miry substrates, while strips of mosquito netting (cast as Spanish moss) are spangled in ghostly swathes and embellished with embroidery—a textured surface to rival the island’s often treacherous topography. “Being on Ossabaw was for me like being at the center of all creation,” Hermansader has said. “It was a place where life was so abundant and varied it was like a living textbook of ecological connections.”

One of the most remarkable images in the exhibition is also one of its humblest: Anne Truitt’s Ossabaw Island, 25 March ’75, a spare abstract drawing of two graphite points with vectors radiating from their centers, washed in fine white acrylic to suggest the divine spark of creation, seeds from which the cosmos might unfold. Fiat lux! (March 25 is also the Feast of the Annunciation.) Enclosed in a vitrine nearby is a first edition of Truitt’s memoir, Daybook: The Journal of an Artist, which she initially conceived as a work of serious literature while staying on Ossabaw in 1975. Something about the island’s rhythms clarified her belief that these habitual diary entries, started the previous year after her furious preparations for two major career retrospectives, might take the shape of a proper text. Published by Pantheon in 1982, it has remained in print ever since, one of the most enduringly popular and beloved artist journals of the twentieth century.

Advertisement

Mythologies of place are always, in some way, about the search for origins—and the exhibition makes much of the notion that Ossabaw was a primordial stage for the drama of humanity’s entanglement with the natural world. A suggestive divot on the shoreline captured in Agnes Denes’s photograph Life Beneath the Surface (1981) recalls a kind of cosmic navel; Leslie Ferst’s vertical glazed clay sculpture The Circumnavigation (1983) evokes an omphalos. The Michigan-born artist Thomas Marker, who served as OIP’s first executive director and was known as the island’s “chief magician,” is represented by two of his drawings from the program’s first year, including Things on Ossabaw (1961): a fanciful yet spare arrangement of amphibians and insects somewhere between loose-leaf doodle and scientific illustration.

Ossabaw stands for the forest primeval in a selection of powerful, large-scale tableaux from Michael Mazur, which convey a sense of womblike enclosure under an intricately scaffolded canopy or within a dense thicket of palmetto leaves. Commissioned by the United States Department of the Interior to represent “the remains of American wilderness,” Mazur’s photorealistic pastels are monumental in scale, nearly immersive, executed with a bravura that might feel suffocating if it weren’t so obsessively finessed. (They contrast satisfyingly with Betsy Cain’s loose, spectral rendering, in oil and Yupo paper, of the endangered longleaf pine.) A suite of Jack Leigh’s striking black-and-white photographs shifts the focus from overall environments to individual specimens: a majestic live oak pierced with shafts of light; a solitary tree at sunset, captivatingly bare and coralline; a palm bent over a fog-enshrouded shore, reaching toward the horizon like an outstretched limb.

The intrepid spirit of Genesis is best channeled in the photography of Helen Hamada and Nancy Marshall. Hamada’s droll self-portraits depict the artist, often nude, seeming to meld with the landscape: barnacled to a tree trunk, face down in the tide. Her group portrait of Genesis members ranged around a gargantuan piece of driftwood is Ossabaw’s unofficial album cover, a distillation of the community’s maverick sensibility. Marshall’s images take a more straightforward approach, presenting subtle yet highly evocative scenes from the treehouse and cookshack alongside a magnificent palladium print that succinctly relays the island’s untainted, prehistoric spirit: a stand of towering palms reflected in a pool of golden water. Irene O’Garden’s macabre ink drawings, entitled Easter Sunday (1981), impart the intensity of island life with sly wit. The series depicts particular moments from the process of raising, slaughtering, and preparing an Easter turkey, with each vignette captioned in girlish cursive: “this drawing was made with a quill from this turkey.”

By 1982 the Wests’ funds were almost entirely depleted, and the programs shut down. While guests continued to visit Ossabaw for shorter periods on a more ad hoc basis, nothing since has approached the largesse of OIP or even Genesis. Today access to the island’s interior remains strictly limited, though entry is permitted by appointment via chartered boat for educational or research purposes. Until her death in 2021, on her 108th birthday, Sandy West waged battle with the State of Georgia whenever they flirted with plans for development or public recreation. “I fought. And I won,” she told a journalist, at the age of ninety-eight, explaining how she managed to keep the island nearly untouched for decades. “Unbelievable. An old crock like me.” Private donations, including from Sandra Bullock, have helped restore various buildings; most recently the Main House and several neighboring structures have been refurbished. Now the newly established Ossabaw Island Residency (a project of the nonprofit ARTS Southeast) prepares to host a fresh cohort of artists, inviting six in the fall and another six in the spring.

Two video works conclude the exhibition. One is an excerpt from Ross McElwee’s landmark documentary Sherman’s March (1985), which focuses, in part, on the filmmaker’s budding romance with Genesis’s codirector Wini Wood, a graduate student in linguistics who expounds charmingly on referential opacity while kneading bread in the cookshack. (She also delivers the classic line, “For a very long time I believed that the only important things in life were linguistics and sex.”) Their relationship blooms and later unravels over hours of languid talk and labor, a delicate flower in the program’s hothouse laboratory that cannot contend with the outside world—or the distressing encroachment, following McElwee’s two-month absence, of Michael the geologist, Wood’s codirector and another suitor.

Allison Janae Hamilton’s short film Venus of Ossabaw (2026), commissioned by Telfair Museums, makes its debut in the galleries, with excerpts projected on the Jepson’s facade for a portion of the exhibition’s run. By turns lyric and feral, the film tracks a young woman’s flight from captivity on an Ossabaw plantation to a life of marronage, tracing her course down the coast of Georgia and into Spanish East Florida—a harsh, unpredictable environment that Hamilton views as both “hostile territory and potential sanctuary.” After encountering a crew of Spanish representatives of the Catholic Church, Venus must decide whether to convert in Saint Augustine and receive conditional manumission through spiritual submission, or to continue into the wilderness, self-possessed and unbroken, proud member of a fugitive tribe.

Hamilton is among a number of artists and academics who, in recent decades, have shed additional light on the Black presence in the Lowcountry. Suzanne Jackson visited the island in 2010 during a brief period when the Ossabaw Island Foundation hosted artists in exchange for artworks that could be sold at its annual fundraiser. Her exuberant and highly expressive watercolors, which often explore the symbolism and ancestral significance of trees, provide a vibrant rejoinder to the sobriety of much traditional Southern landscape painting. Rashod Taylor’s crepuscular tintypes achieve a pleasing thickness of atmosphere, heavy with mood and shadow, while Tyrone Mitchell’s Buzzard Vine (1983) is a wry surrealist object that extracts a visual riddle from the island, presenting a length of braided, varnished vine to mark the moment from his stay when a buzzard defecated on his head.

The exhibition is accompanied by a richly illustrated catalog with insightful contributions from, among others, the writer and curator Thomas Lax—who considers the aesthetic influence of the barrier islands and Gullah Geechee culture on artists like Jackson, Beverly Buchanan, Cameron Rowland, and Julie Dash—and Wini Wood, the young linguist of Sherman’s March. (She did, in fact, marry Michael.) This polyphonic approach further underscores the variety of connections that Sandy promoted on Ossabaw between humans and the natural world, and among practitioners across disciplines—a distinctly nonhierarchical mode of engagement that the writer Megan Mayhew Bergman astutely describes as “ecofeminist” avant la lettre.

What is Ossabaw’s legacy today? The Wests’ relationship to the island stands in stark contrast to the reigning economic paradigm in the US, which fetishizes efficiency at all costs and treats the earth as an endlessly plunderable resource for capital accumulation. But the Wests always privileged the magical over the practical. “Could it have all been done smarter? Probably,” the Wests’ son later reflected on the family’s financial struggles. “Could it have been done better? I don’t think so.”

The story of Ossabaw is a kind of miracle: a proudly eccentric heiress with haughty disdain for convention lavishes her fortune on the leading thinkers and makers of her time, splurging on their freedom so they can accomplish extraordinary feats of imagination. If the results of the Wests’ noblesse oblige are impossible to measure, it might be because their reward is beyond remuneration. One of the exhibition’s coups is to give concrete form to the many ways that a direct experience of wilderness can influence artistic and intellectual endeavor. “All I wanted to do is give people a place that had no demands on them,” Sandy once said. “I didn’t care what they did here. I cared what the island did to them.”

entries.title: The Cruel and the Frail

entries.content:
This is part of a series of essays drawn from the Georgetown Global Dialogues, an ongoing program convening writers and intellectuals, many from the Global South, to discuss ways of confronting our current political crises. The previous installment can be found here.

“What is happening in the world today,” Thomas Merton wrote to Czesław Miłosz in 1959, responding to the latter’s book The Captive Mind, “is a wholesale collapse of man’s capacity to love.” Merton did not believe in the cold war’s strident moral opposition between the free and unfree worlds. Whether in the West or in the East, he wrote to Miłosz, “one lives in a state of constant bewilderment and fear.” For Merton, this helplessness was a distinctive condition of man “at the moment of his greatest power over things other than himself,” and there was no easy release from it. But he knew, too, that “the only thing that is to be regretted without qualification is for a man to adapt perfectly to totalitarian society. Then he is indeed beyond hope.”

That inadvertent adaptation to a pernicious social reality is a greater danger for many more people today, as they settle deeper into a state of constant bewilderment and fear. The forces of war and authoritarianism are stronger, and now visibly present in established democracies as much as elsewhere. All this has engendered a widespread sense of powerlessness. Efforts to mobilize civil society, nationally and transnationally, against encroaching regimes of cruelty and injustice are undermined by dysfunctional political institutions and the flood of AI-generated misinformation on social media and even in the news.

It has also become clear that the philosophy of liberal individualism offers little protection against such disorder, or against the fears—and realities—of abandonment, dispossession, and decline that afflict many in a vast and seemingly incomprehensible world. On the contrary: the conventional liberal vision of self-empowering rational individuals pursuing their own interests and personal flourishing seems disturbingly similar to the dominant tenets of a cynical realism that celebrates self-seeking actors pursuing power and wealth by all necessary means.

But then the anthropological vision underpinning the liberal model of human society was always limited. The world’s great philosophical and spiritual traditions have always presupposed that human beings are not autonomous, self-interested actors. Rather, we are frail, error-prone, vulnerable, and dependent. Born into groups—families, tribes, linguistic communities, and nations—we are bound to one another by ties of mutual responsibility. Prone to hatred and resentment, we are also capable of sympathy, empathy, and even love, of wanting and pursuing the good of others, whether family or community members, fellow citizens we will never meet, or human beings on the other side of the planet.

Today, it is imperative that we move beyond the modern ideologies of individual empowerment that increasingly foster political anarchy and moral nihilism, and find new sources of transnational solidarity against the forces of violence and injustice. To reactivate hope, we need to draw on the philosophical and spiritual traditions that acknowledge our frailty and mutual dependence as human beings, and our capacity for love, fellow-feeling, and compassion.

Those who benefit materially from the status quo of corrupted liberal individualism will resist such a shift; and it will hardly take place quickly or extensively. But who can doubt that some different modes of thinking and feeling are desperately needed? Over the past year, the Georgetown Global Dialogues, which we direct together, have explored resources for solidarity still available to us during a worldwide political and moral breakdown.

Last June, leading writers, including Juan Gabriel Vásquez, Javier Cercas, Zadie Smith, Naomi Klein, Eva Menasse, and Hisham Matar, came together in Rome to engage with Pope Francis’s ideas about human fraternity and a “culture of encounter.” At our gathering in Spain this past November, hosted by Judit Carrera and the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona, Marina Garcés, Mohsin Hamid, Nesrine Malik, Ece Temelkuran, and many others addressed the themes of cruelty and powerlessness—and considered ways to break the impasse of fear and bewilderment by recognizing our shared vulnerability. —Thomas Banchoff and Pankaj Mishra

Accepting Defeat
Ece Temelkuran

As global fascism creeps across the planet, the intellect seeks refuge—a country or a city where it is safe. When fascism first hit the world there was “America,” not only a land to escape to but also an idea, a torch for “the wretched refuse of your teeming shore,” a land for “the homeless, tempest-tost.” Today, the second time around, even American intellectuals are considering exile, tasting “how salt the savour is of others’ bread,” as Dante once wrote. Yet today we know that there is nowhere to run.

Intellectuals and academics around the world, even in the West, are in survival mode. Our minds have begun to understand what has long been clear to refugees from Syria or Central America or so many other places where life has been made untenable. We are already unhomed by fascism, and critical thought is becoming homeless, a vulnerable fugitive. We know that if we are to survive and protect critical thought, we will have to be in solidarity. So why is that not happening? What is the moral or political obstacle preventing us from lifting our eyes and perceiving our common plight?

Advertisement

For one, too many of us still think that we can survive on our own. This kind of neoliberal morality, the sense of “going it alone,” is far more deeply buried in us than we’d like to believe, a kind of moral contamination. The second reason for our current moral precarity is arrogance. To begin to build solidarity, we must acknowledge our powerlessness. We have to come to terms with our defeat, and this will require radical humility. “Defeat” is not a glamorous word; it is almost taboo in the vocabulary of political movements. Yet in a world where the worship of the winner reigns and people take cynical glee in others’ misfortunes, acknowledging defeat carries a moral and emotional charge, a transformative potential. Defeat can liberate us from a posture we have kept up for too long—of pride in place of dignity, of passivity instead of humility. Only when we truly accept that it is human to lose, and noble to try anyway, can we find the bravery our circumstances require.

The poetic leap intellectuals need to make to be in reality, to live in the here and now, can only happen when we are brave enough to accept that there is no going back to the old homes of intellect. We need to come to terms with the fact that critical thought in today’s world is in retreat. Contrary to what many people may think, it is not this cold reality that will break us. What exhausts us is our self-imposed obligation to pretend that we are still in the old reality where our voices mattered. The acceptance of this defeat brings with it a much-needed humility, a willingness to face reality together, and a stronger bond.

This is how refugees survive. As an exile, I can say that, when homeless, one can only survive by accepting with radical realism that life is here and now, and that home can only be other people. When you accept this reality the concept of solidarity shifts from being a nice thought to being the only means of survival. The true meaning of humility, integrity, and, if I may say, human love surfaces. Fraternity will illuminate the path we must follow.

After accepting defeat, don’t stare into the black hole of cynicism; look at one another. Only by looking at one another can we see the poetic power of our weaknesses and comprehend how big a majority we are. Safety is no longer in places; refuge can only be found in others. As a Syrian refugee who had crossed the Mediterranean in a dinghy once said to me, “Don’t look at the waves at night. You should look at your companions’ faces to believe.”

These reflections are adapted from Ece Temelkuran’s remarks in a conversation with Pankaj Mishra, Hisham Matar, and Marina Garcés on Building Solidarity in a Fragmented Culture.

Fear and Love in Politics
Mohsin Hamid

At this moment of powerlessness and confusion, as we look for solidarity and ways forward, the physical sciences might be an unexpected ally. Unexpected, because the sciences are often regarded as closely aligned with the industrial and technocratic ideologies that we blame for much of our current predicament.

Our dominant philosophies have been constructed on the basis of a particular understanding of science, one that formed during the Enlightenment. In such a model there was very little space for mystery. All things could be reduced to cause and effect, to matter and motion. Having conceived of the universe in this way, it made sense to construct our economic institutions similarly, on the basis of rational agents seeking to maximize their individual utilities. This is the underpinning of market capitalism as we know it today.

Yet more recent scientific developments have revealed that our Enlightenment understanding was flawed. Gravity, for example, is not the simple force we imagined it to be, but rather bends time itself. Our seemingly rational choices might actually be illusions, our conscious mammalian minds retroactively superimposing narratives on actions previously and unknowably determined in the reptilian recesses of our brains. Relativity and quantum theory, our models of the very large and the very small, are mathematically incompatible. The science is getting very weird.

We have been clinging to outdated and overly simplistic notions of what a human being is, what an economy and a society are, what the universe is. If we wish to grapple with the much more complex realities that the modern sciences suggest, we will have to update our perspectives. We will, as our ancient ancestors did, have to contend with paradox, with the nonrational, with the inexpressible. Now, once again, we have no choice but to reckon with mystery. Since our present ordering of the world is failing us in so many ways, a radical reconsideration of its foundations should be a source of hope.

Advertisement

Standing in the way of such hope is our profound sense of fear. We live in a world of enormous material abundance, in aggregate. We live longer and eat more calories, on average, than our forebears did. Yes, we face a multitude of crises—political, economic, environmental, cultural, personal. But ours are not the first generations to do so. Instead it is possible that our expansive, pervasive sense of fear, or rather the preconditions for our sense of fear, are in fact rooted in the self-centered philosophies, economies, and belief systems that we have built.

We are trapped inside our conviction of the utter centrality of self. For once we reckon, as we are forced to, with the fact that we all die, that our self is going to end, we are confronted with a terrible horror. Unless we find ways to inoculate ourselves against this horror, we are predisposed to excessive fear. And this excessive fear then gives birth to so much of the politics, and so many of the crises, that we see around us.

So it is worth considering the ways that we have found to address such fears throughout history. One of the most powerful is love. A love that surmounts fear has been articulated in many different traditions. Pope Francis wrote about a radical political love in the Catholic tradition; in the Sufi tradition, in the part of the world that I come from, the poets tell us that through love we can achieve a form of transcendence.

Exactly what kind of love are Pope Francis and the Sufis referring to? They are not referring to love as we commonly use the term today, as a desire for possession. Not love that reaffirms the self. Not love that says I love you only because you make me less lonely, but rather the love that says I love you because I wish you to be less lonely. A love that decenters the self.

We live in a time of fear, and therefore in a time of hate, and so it is natural to talk about the need for tolerance. But tolerance is such a tepid thing. The true excitement in the condition of being different, together, is that it opens up the possibility of cross-fertilization, of two different things coming together and making something new.  

If our old scientific certainties sought to banish mystery, our present era of uncertainty is ushering mystery back in. Among our great mysteries is the human capacity for love. I can think of nothing more hopeful than the possibility that love across differences will give birth to the new ideas that we will require to grapple with the future.

These reflections are adapted from Mohsin Hamid’s remarks in a conversation with Thomas Banchoff; Fr. Antonio Spadaro, SJ; and Mar Griera on Fraternity/Solidarity: Secular and Religious Perspectives.

Political Cruelty
Nesrine Malik

Cruelty has always been part of human nature and part of politics. What is new is the way it has entered into the mainstream of our global era. Increasingly, cruelty has become both the language of politics and the way it is transacted.

It is not enough just to pass a law against immigration. It is not enough to pass a law to deprive people of government benefits for their children. It is not enough to reverse movements for racial and gender equality. You must also shout about it. You must also humiliate the people who you are fighting. You must, in some instances, as in the US and UK, parade them in shackles and even render them in illustrations and cartoons for people to mock.

This is not a cruelty with a clear ideological or practical purpose. It is cruelty for its own sake. As Adam Serwer put it in a memorable essay written during the first Trump administration: “the cruelty is the point.” Not a byproduct of policy, but the essence and purpose of it.

How has cruelty come to be the point? This is not just about dictatorships or demagogues. Cruelty has become a necessary way of transacting politics because politics in so many countries has reached a dead end. Over the last four decades much of the promise, hope, and progress that once seemed achievable through politics has been curtailed. Public spaces have become diminished, our extended families have become fractured, the price of housing has risen, and many of us live in smaller and smaller spaces, siloed from one another. We have less and less from our governments—in the way of both the broad safety net that the state can offer and the basic expectation of a dignified life. You are going to have to hustle and scramble and struggle to be able to buy a home, secure safe schooling for your children, afford health care, and die with dignity. Over the past forty years capitalist economies have become mean and tightfisted.

So what can politicians offer when they cannot promise people housing, health care, clean streets, not to mention aspirations? They can’t even promise the status quo, can’t even say that life is going to stay as it is, because in fact it is going to get worse. With no promises to offer, politicians start pointing to others who they claim are responsible for your dismal fate, others who will make things worse in the future if we do not get rid of them.

I call this the exploitation of scarcity. Instead of addressing the root causes of scarcity, how our economics and politics are arranged, policymakers discuss immigrants, people on benefits, racial minorities, single mothers, the “other.” Or in the UK, increasingly: Muslims.

To a politician, cruelty is very useful. What do they have to gain from explaining that the deregulation that began in the 1970s is responsible for contemporary labor insecurity? Voters cannot do anything easy or immediate with that information. But if you tell them an immigrant is taking their job, they can feel that and act on it. There is a feedback loop between those who want quick, satisfying, visceral answers; the politicians who feed them silver-bullet solutions; and the people who are caught in the middle, humiliated and vilified. Cruelty becomes a circus-like performance in which we all participate—ambient, atmospheric cruelty, toward “the other,” the minor, the weaker, the individual who is lower down the hierarchy.

It is nothing short of a miracle that amid such cruel conditions one can still find compassion, bravery, and the insistence on seeing the humanity of others. I always think of the similarities across the revolutionary spaces I have experienced across the Arab World, how they all share an overflowing of solidarity, fraternity, and artistic expression. I found strong echoes of that at the student protests for Gaza across campuses in the UK and the US in 2023 and 2024, as well as the antiracist counterprotests against far-right rallies in the UK last summer.

The onslaught of cruelty and its methods is formidable, but it is a warping of human nature, rather than the natural expression of it. Sabotaging cruelty requires only that a few people gather and talk, and then invite a few more people to do the same. I’m actually quite hopeful. To break the spell of cruelty, we need understanding and community-making, we need to go out into the physical world and say that it doesn’t have to be this way.

These reflections are adapted from Nesrine Malik’s remarks in a conversation with Verónica Gago, Edurne Portela, and Joseba Elola on Calling Out Cruelty.

Beyond Solidarity
Marina Garcés

On October 29, 2024, it rained heavily in the Valencia region, in the east of Spain. It has always rained “wrong” in Valencia, too much in too short a time. But according to official figures, on this one day, what with the effects of climate change and excessive construction on flood-prone ground, 232 people drowned, a majority of the 335 people who died due to storms and flooding in all of Europe that year.

Another lethal factor, alongside the climate emergency and the excesses of urbanization, was the inertness of the denialist, populist Valencian government, which downplayed the seriousness of the disaster, failed to issue warnings, and left the people to fend for themselves. In Spain’s worst flood in modern history, only ordinary people came out to save their neighbors, and for weeks citizens from around Valencia and the rest of Spain took the lead in cleaning up the mud and recovering bodies. Meanwhile politicians squabbled and administrations blamed each other. Announcing his resignation on the first anniversary of the catastrophe, the former Valencian president, Carlos Mazón, who was directly responsible for the negligent rescue efforts, proclaimed, “The images of solidarity are the greatest ray of hope these days.”

These words would be heartwarming if they hadn’t already been discredited by a year of death, lies, and despair. What solidarity could he be talking about, this president who had to resign the day after the floods, and who is now being prosecuted?

I’m raising this question because I think it is important to listen to words, to carefully analyze them. Some words are frequently used to cover up the truth and, at the same time, to manipulate people’s emotions. “Solidarity” can be one of these words. Then it becomes dangerous.

It was precisely during those terrible weeks, when thousands and thousands of people went to Valencia to help, that a slogan spread by word of mouth and on social media: “Only the people can save the people.” It’s a catchphrase that spurred on rescue groups, but it is also ambiguous. Which people did it refer to? Was it appealing to the strength of solidarity, organized horizontally among equals, as the bedrock of a robust and well-structured society? Or did it identify the people as a force that rises from the rubble of political institutions when they shirk their responsibilities—an idea with reactionary potential? It soon became clear that the slogan was being employed by the formal and informal organizations of the far right, from political parties to football clubs.

“Solidarity” can be used to dodge responsibilities, and to avoid the use of other more committed words, like “justice,” “equality,” and “dignity.” Beyond the charitable gestures with which the rich of the world nourish their consciences, and beyond the collective scenes of people rescuing themselves, solidarity as a political value is about understanding life as a shared problem. Acting in solidarity isn’t just helping. Acting in solidarity means struggling together and creating, with others, the conditions for a more dignified, more just life.

Understanding life as a shared problem means learning, over again and newly, to say “we.” The rich supremacist world shields itself by referring to the rest of the world in the third person: them, the poor; them, the migrants; them, the terrorists. Inside and outside the West, the walls are growing ever higher, separating those who can drown from those who are still privileged enough to save themselves and their privatized futures. Solidarity doesn’t mean lamenting, getting scared, or feeling sorry for ourselves. It means starting, yet again, to tear down these walls together.

These reflections are adapted from Marina Garcés’s remarks in a conversation with Pankaj Mishra, Ece Temelkuran, and Pankaj Mishra on Building Solidarity in a Fragmented Culture.

entries.content:
“I Liked Rex”: this is the title of the title story in Diane Williams’s new collection. These three words, subject, verb, and object, form a complete sentence, one that echoes a line from the famous mid-century primer See Spot Run. Spot was a dog. Might Rex be one, too? In a sense, he is: a sly dog, a dirty dog; a big, handsome, disreputable man, prone to wandering off in search of fresh adventure, then sniffing his way back home. When the narrator of “I Liked Rex” sees him again, after one of his long absences, she observes that he has dressed the part: “He wore a heavy wool suit I’d never seen before—a glen-plaid houndstooth check—and next, in bed, I thought his very pink privates were meant to be some cheery dessert.” How easy it is for Rex to cut through her sexual defenses. Against him, she has none.

What she has, instead, is a passion for detail and a savage talent for metaphor. That glen-plaid houndstooth check suit and, underneath it, those very pink privates—I imagine them as two melting scoops of strawberry ice cream—flesh out a man at once self-serious and impossible to take seriously. The effect of this finely wrought sentence is to depose Rex, to neuter this dog-man. His charms are consigned to the past tense. He elicits the mildest emotion, liking, not loving, even as the narrator pants in bed with him. Near the end of the story, she sits on a cliff and looks down at a seaside village while stroking another dog, her pet sheltie. She celebrates her freedom to perceive the world below however she wishes:

True, we are prone to sea storms and landslides, but this village also provides a panoramic view, amusements, and benefits, as well as a horrid gorge. But don’t let’s look at that. Let’s be happy.

Let us enjoy our holidays and let us fall for or swear by whatever we want to—because people really like to.

The marvelous fiction of Diane Williams is constructed on a single epic theme: “The loss of paradise keeps happening.” All the qualities that distinguish her stories follow from it. There is usually a woman in the story, its narrator, who risks being ruined by one man or torn between two, all with vaguely absurd names: “Rex” or “Fabio” or “Mr. Casanova.” There is a sexual encounter, a suspended moment of ecstasy, followed by a rude disappointment, the betrayal of an ideal—and, out of this betrayal, the revelation of a moral or a maxim, a solemn covenant forged between the narrator and her reader, like “let us fall for or swear by whatever we want to.” Paradise is regained. A state of languid serenity settles in—but it lasts only until the page is turned, and the next story greets us, with a bold, startling title. This is the ground that Williams has tilled for nearly forty years, from her first story collection, This Is About the Body, the Mind, the Soul, the World, Time, and Fate, to I Liked Rex, her twelfth and, to my mind, her most balanced.

From this ground, her stories rise like so many private chapels, small, secretive, poised, and richly ornamented. Their architecture, her style, is their singular achievement. Her paragraphs are usually one sentence, sometimes two, rarely three. Her sentences are built around her uncommonly disciplined syntax; on nouns and adjectives of unique significance, joined to one another by plainspoken verbs, with almost no adverbs in sight, the exceptions being the casual comic intensifiers, such as Rex’s “very pink privates,” or little radiances of sexual and spiritual activity. The narrator of the story “Oh, to Be Able to Inspire Sex Love” arrives at an orgy, uninvited, only to fall asleep. When she leaves, she thinks, “I go out, most prayerfully, seductively.” Williams’s discipline falters only in matters typographical. There, she reveals her weakness for double and triple dashes, for italics, for exclamations and exclamation marks, scattered liberally across the page and with great charm. “Oh!” she gasps, over and over again. One feels that she is often surprised—or perhaps terrified—by the hidden currents of her own mind, and that her syntax lets those emotions find the surest path onto the page.

Nouns are the seat of Williams’s power, and they live at extremes; they are either wholly abstract or wholly particular. In her abstract mode, her stories are filled with scantily clad archetypes. “The man entered the lady’s house as if it were the most natural thing for him to do,” begins the story “There You Go.” Her narrators speak elliptically, whether from confusion or a sense of discretion, it is difficult to know. “Maybe I went with somebody I knew,” the central character of “Oh, to Be Able to Inspire Sex Love” recalls of the orgy she crashed. “I felt breath on the top of my head as someone dislodged himself.” They invoke dignity, bravery, truth, and love as if these concepts were as tangible and sturdy as my dining-room table. In the particular mode, her narrators fixate on proper nouns, on alliterative names, like “Seth Sharples” or “Miles Macbeth,” or luxurious brands: a Tiffany picture frame, a Chanel chiffon scarf, a Chloraseptic Max Wild Berry Sore Throat Lozenge. Often, a noun will press a parade of adjectives into its service, as if to insist that here—right here!—is where the reader must enter the sensual world of the story; where she can inhale the “pearly shell ginger blossoms” in a tropical garden; fiddle with the “lapis and carnelian” in a string of beads or the “gold-colored hairpins” in a woman’s updo; or fondle “a piece of a shell—veined, and slick as if lacquered—nearly a dugout-canoe shape” that a man finds in his pocket. These tightly bound noun phrases are where her impulse to describe meets the straitjacket of her style.

Advertisement

Their meeting is what gives her stories the flash and feeling of dreams. The hard, bright detail lifted to the light of consciousness gains its clarity from the shadows that loom behind it, from everything that must be repressed in waking life. Like dreams, the stories place their events in no natural order or proportion. They are free-associative, bounding between the past and the present, between the throwaway detail and the fatal outcry. “This is dreamland to her—although she does have, on her torso, that pesky parapsoriasis,” the narrator of the story “For Pity’s Sake” observes of an old woman called Mrs. Goodenough. Her narrators have little interest in creating believable characters—allegorical ones will do just fine—or in tracing the fixed causalities of plot. “Must there really be a need for harsh realism?” one of them wonders. Yet there is nothing chaotic about a story by Williams. Not an image feels false. Not a comma is out of place. From the first story to the last, her voice holds as steady as an oracle’s.

Williams is a single-minded writer, faithful to her particular form and her themes. Recently, in a used book store, I found a galley of her first collection, This Is About the Body, the Mind, the Soul, the World, Time, and Fate, from 1990. The title was borrowed from a book she found on her shelf, The Origins of European Thought: About the Body, the Mind, the Soul, the World, Time and Fate. Using it declared her high ambition, she told me—her intent to “piss with the big dogs,” including her former teacher, Gordon Lish. The second story in the collection is called “The Nature of the Miracle.” Here is its beginning:

The green glass bottle rolled into, rolled out of my arms, out of my hands, and then exploded, just as it should, when it hits our bluestone floor, and spreads itself, and sparkling water, on the territory it was able to cover from our refrigerator to the back door.

The bottle used to fit tightly in my hand, easily, by the neck, and the way one thing leads to another in my mind, this means I should run away from my marriage.

Why one thing leads to another in one’s mind is often mysterious. There is, of course, no logical reason why a bottle slipping out of your hand means that you should run away from your marriage. But if the image of that bottle rolling, exploding, and spreading itself is rendered with sufficient violence and awe, then it imposes its own meaning. “Everything means something, or it does not,” Williams writes in “The Uncanny.” This has been her aim in each collection: to make everything, no matter how trivial, mean something. As her style has become more assured, she has taken greater risks. She has stretched the connection between her images and what they mean to the breaking point, courting a kind of mysticism, and, at times, a madness.

Williams and I have been friends since I wrote about her collected stories for this magazine. I like to visit her at home, where we drink tea and talk, and she lends me her books; I have her copy of Hotel du Lac and intend to return it one day very soon. Some of my happiest moments have been spent watching her work as an editor of NOON, the annual magazine of short fiction that she founded in 2000. She works as if in a trance, with an absorbed and exacting confidence. I have seen her carve, from a slab of a text, a single paragraph or sentence, chiseling its language into a state of muscular perfection. The first time it happened, I was reminded of an apocryphal story about a famous sculptor. He claimed that the marble blocks he hauled from the quarry already contained his figures inside; his only task was to liberate them. To liberate the essence of a story from its padding—the who, what, where, when, and why of exposition—is a delicate undertaking. It risks insensitivity, cruelty even. But, in Williams’s hands, it is an invitation for the writer to look the reader dead in the eye and speak the naked truth. And her writers, I suspect, must welcome the pleasure of supplication, the abandonment of their ego to the forceful, but careful, will of another.

Advertisement

Under her editorship, a distinct strain of contemporary writing has emerged from the pages of NOON, which has featured the work of Lydia Davis, Christine Schutt, Dawn Raffel, Danielle Dutton, Kathryn Scanlan, Lucie Elven, Deb Olin Unferth, Rita Bullwinkel, and many others I admire. Some have called it minimalism, thinking, perhaps, of the cold shadow cast by Lish over the short story. But the stories that Williams edits have little in common with the bare, withholding style of, for instance, Raymond Carver, or his obsession with a wounded American masculinity; the loss of paradise in NOON is, primarily if not exclusively, a wise woman’s concern. Others have described Williams as the “godmother of flash fiction.” But that term has no discernible meaning, no purchase on the aesthetic features of these stories or the experience of reading them. They are intricate and demanding, fastidious to the point of being fussy—at moments self-consciously, humorously so. Their humor hinges on the sharp sense of disproportion between the stories’ parts and their whole. The details they lavish their attentions on appear too specific, too extravagant, and too dazzling for the narrative that encloses them, which, by comparison, appears undeveloped in the conventional terms of character and plot. Their narrators tend to speak in epigrams and aphorisms, to dispatch prophecies to the reader and prayers to someone up above. They aim to capture both the gorgeous surfaces of human life and the mysterious worlds beyond, squeezing the universe into a page or two that contains at once too much and not enough. This is not minimalism; far from it. Call it miniaturism.

In NOON’s miniaturism, one can hear the last laugh of modernism’s avant-garde, a comic blend of Gertrude Stein’s rigor, Djuna Barnes’s decadence, and Wallace Stevens’s philosophical grandeur, laced with a cheerful sexual frankness that belongs to Williams, and Williams alone. But one can also detect notes of anxiety, especially in her stories’ metafictional eruptions. “Yes, okay, but this story, as yet—is just not good enough!” a narrator exclaims. “Oh, just sum it up!” cries another. The story “The Greatest Experience” anticipates that its readers will want characters with more transparent motives: “In this chapter, at some point, we should seek to understand these people, as if we could say to them—We have been talking about you. Mind if we ask you a few questions?” The story “Diane!” begins with bafflement and alarm about how characters are created:

What in the world will her name be? Diane!

I should not hurt anybody else I know with this story.

I hope she is not too fake.

The narrators of these stories ventriloquize the typically anxious editor, the person responsible for worrying that the reader might want more—more backstory, more interiority, more sympathy, more reality. But there is no need to worry. There is more than enough harsh realism to go around. There are plenty of conventional people and plenty of conventional stories about the loss of paradise. Most of us live through it at least once, if not twice, and it usually lasts longer than we would like. Let it be brief and shocking and full of wonder, Williams says. Then, let us move on to the next story, and the next one, and the one after that!

entries.title: The Other Donald
entries.summary: A dispatch from the Art Editor
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On a recent Friday afternoon, I visited the Judd Foundation building at 101 Spring Street and was taken on a tour of the space by their new director of design, Alexandra Cunningham Cameron.

Donald Judd bought the building in 1968. He lived and worked there (and in his other residences in Texas and Switzerland) until his death at sixty-five, in 1994. Like his carefully constructed art, there are many precise details to admire at the foundation. I particularly enjoyed the vast wooden ceiling on the third floor, which mirrors the planks on the floor below, and the baseboards Judd installed on the top level, which give the space a quiet domestic touch. Each spoon and trivet felt like a larger part of his practice, a portrait of the artist in boots and books, pots and pans.

Our Summer Issue cover is by Lisa Hanawalt, the funny-as-all-heck cartoonist and animator behind the brilliant shows Tuca and Bertie and BoJack Horseman, as well as hilarious illustrated books like Hot Dog Taste Test (2016) and, most recently, I Can’t Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex.

She sent a handful of sketches for the cover, and we chose a rooftop rendezvous, set during the “dimity, duskety hour,” as Hanwalt described it. Earlier this month, I interviewed Hanawalt about the cover and her practice.

Matthew Aucoin wrote about the composer Dylan Mattingly, and James McMullan sent in a lively portrait in profile, with dancing musical notation streaming out behind Mattingly. I asked Harriet Lee-Merrion to take on Anahid Nersessian’s review of Killing Spree, by the poet Jorie Graham. Lee-Merrion wrote that she wanted to show Graham’s “wonderful white hair, contrasting to a big black sweater (since in pictures she seems to wear black attire).”

Yann Kebbi drew the writer John Lanchester for Laura Marsh’s essay about his latest novel, Look What You Made Me Do. In Kebbi’s portrait, Lanchester’s head seems to glow, animated perhaps by the themes of surveillance, crypto, and online disturbance that Marsh details in her review. For David Cole on Trump’s interference with and influence on the Supreme Court, I turned to designer Paul Sahre, who has done great political work for us before. He inserted a glowering, berobed Trump alongside the justices in their official SCOTUS group portrait.

Deborah Eisenberg wrote about the German postwar novelist Wolfgang Koeppen, and I asked the Berlin-based illustrator Henning Wagenbreth for a portrait. He had coincidentally visited Koeppen’s birthplace, Greifswald, two weeks earlier. He drew Koeppen in Munich amid the ruins of World War II, surrounded by pigeons. He also included, he explained to me, “some stones/rubble on the ground because at the end of [one of Koeppen’s] novels an American soldier will be stoned because of false allegations.”

The series art, titled “Conversations with Pens,” is by Ginger Sorbara, a Toronto-based architect and designer.

It was a relief to think of the greatness of one Donald in contrast to another. Judd’s spaces, symmetries, and collections left me with a feeling of peace and solidity, a rare thing in a summer of destabilizing news.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I first read Fortress Besieged as a teenager, when the novel, originally published in 1947 and out of print for decades, became a bestseller in China after it was adapted into a TV series in 1990. The book was so popular that its characters quickly became, in the public imagination, types—in fact, archetypes—as though a mere reference to the name of this or that character was enough to summarize the essence of an acquaintance or a family member. Memorable lines from the novel circulated. An old woman selling steamed buns by the roadside was likely to repeat to a young couple pondering her goods that “if men don’t get enough to eat, they’ll get irritable”—words spoken by Sun Jou-chia, a Vera Rostova–like character who has won a competi­tion to become the wife of Fang Hung-chien, the hero of the novel, only to have the same epiphany as Vera did in War and Peace, that men are more or less children, to be put up with and to be put under discipline. A high school student could cite the epigraph of the novel to a friend—“Marriage is like a fortress besieged: those who are out­side want to get in, and those who are inside want to get out”—and surmise that the metaphor would apply to more situations than mar­riage; life itself must be like a fortress besieged. (I was one of those philosophizing teenagers.)

Fortress Besieged is reputed to have sold ten million copies in China since it came back in print. Written by the literary scholar Qian Zhongshu, the novel was published before communism took over, which exempted it from the censorship and state intervention that was a common fate of much Chinese literature written in the second half of the twentieth century. To two generations of readers fed on party-sanctioned propaganda, it brought the freshest air.

It seemed a miracle that the book existed at all. It takes place in 1937 and 1938, at the beginning of the eight-year Sino-Japanese War. My elders, coming from the same province as the Fang family, passed down stories that were essen­tial to my understanding of that history: my great-grandfather, the owner of a fabric shop with a lame leg, was put to hard labor by the Japanese and haphazardly executed because his disability made him an inefficient worker; my uncle, eight years old, went out with a playmate to the field and returned in the evening to find that his fam­ily, unable to locate him on the day of an imminent invasion, had fled without him. Until his old age he could not forget his months of living as a vagabond in the heavily bombed country.

We are not the only family bearing such a history. A family friend once handed me a self-published memoir by her sister relating that their grandfather, a doctor of Western medicine, was betrayed by a nephew, a collaborator with the Japanese; the doctor was arrested and tortured, the family broken up. A neighbor in Beijing once told me all her wartime memories, including being thrown down into a well along with a cousin—they were young girls then—by their elders for fear that they would be captured and raped by the Japanese. “Here,” the old woman pointed to a dent in her hairline, “you can feel the scar. We were lucky that there was some water in the well but not too much.”

Wartime tragedies and atrocities happen in Fortress Besieged but mostly offstage, alluded to without being given a direct look. The brutal early months of the war, “from the retreat from Shanghai to the fall of Nanking,” flash by in little more than a paragraph. More vividly evoked are the effects of the fighting on the conditions of daily life in occupied Shanghai, one of the novel’s primary settings, where by the end of the book slums are proliferating “like ringworm” and commodity prices are rising “like a kite with its string broken in the wind.”

But most of the novel’s attention goes to the characters as they eat, drink, flirt, write mediocre poetry, dis­cuss Western and Eastern philosophies, and stab one another in the back with puny, metaphorical knives for insubstantial gain and petty revenge. The civilian life in the novel—in Hong Kong, in Shanghai, and in a provincial town where a university is assembled halfheartedly to accommodate the refugee students from occupied regions—echoes the society life of Moscow and Saint Petersburg in War and Peace. The fiercest battles happen in drawing rooms or at dinner tables; close combat—carried out in words and gestures instead of with bay­onets or sabers—doesn’t draw blood but kills off people’s spirits.

That people could live in an entirely different manner through wartime, largely untouched, was a revelation to me when I first read Fortress Besieged. It’s like War and Peace without the war. Fang Hung-chien is the quintessential superfluous character. There is a bit of Pierre’s naiveté in him, but none of Pierre’s curiosity or idealism. We follow him as he returns from “studying abroad,” having secured a fake diploma from an Irish con man in New York, and embroils himself in a love triangle in Shanghai, leading on an actual Ph.D. recipient named Miss Su while pining for her younger cousin, Miss T’ang:

Advertisement

Waiting for him to make his formal declaration of love, Miss Su inwardly faulted him for being so frivolous and tardy; he, on the other hand, was waiting for a chance to explain that he did not love her, and wished he weren’t so tenderhearted and could be courageous enough to cut the Gordian knot. Every time he went to the Sus, he came away reproaching himself for having gone one more time and talked so much again. He gradually realized that he was what Westerners called a “moral weakling,” and was worried that Miss T’ang would detect this major flaw in his character.

Eventually, after falling out of favor with both women, he gets a temporary job at the fictional National San Lü University, where he blunders his way into the ill-fated marriage that takes up the book’s last chapters. (“Though in the heat of anger they might find quarreling a great relief, when the quarrel was over they both felt exhausted and empty, the feeling one gets at the end of the opera or when one wakes from a drunken sleep.”) Reflecting on the prospect of meeting his former crush, he realizes how many of his old selves he no longer recognizes:

He had buried some of his dead selves in his memory, erected a monument to them, and occasionally paid them homage, such as by a moment of feeling for T’ang Hsiao-fu. Others seemed to have died by the wayside and been left there to rot and decompose or be devoured by birds and beasts—but never to be completely obliterated, such as the self which had bought the diploma from the Irishman.

There is a hint of Hamlet’s indecision in Fang, but he is a Hamlet without the pressure to take any revenge for a mother country being pillaged and raped, and his entire tragedy, in the end, is to have married the wrong woman. One supposes that, had Hamlet lived on, his marriage to Ophelia could hardly have been a happy one.

Everywhere Fang goes he comes across new spectacles of folly and pretension. As a sideline, a professor of literature runs a racketeering business. A university president speaks like a saint but covets other people’s wives. Young women strive to entrap a husband, like Jane Austen characters. Married women manipulate and cheat on their husbands, some skillfully and others as wistfully as Emma Bovary. Very few books force Chinese readers to so directly confront their own casual bigotry, calculated cruelty, and ingenuity for, as one idiom has it, pomp and vain­glory in the space within the shell of a snail.

Fortress Besieged is widely praised as a masterpiece of satire. Its lineage within Chinese literature traces back to The Scholars by Wu Jingzi (1701–1754) and Officialdom Unmasked by Li Baojia (1867–1906), two well-known Qing Dynasty novels. The vivid portraits of characters of various social classes in both books offered much entertainment when we studied excerpts from them in middle and high school. Yet, few of us, I dare say, recognized the incarnations of those seventeenth- and eighteenth-century characters in our own lives: a chairwoman of the neighborhood association who seemed to have unlimited power (in my family’s case, she and her team liked to break into our apartment in the middle of the night, looking for an American or Taiwanese spy, because one of my uncles fled to Taiwan after 1949); a butcher who took in the rationing ticket for meat and then decided, depending on his mood, whether to cut a thin and yet decent slice or just a chunk of fat; or a woman who sat in front of the public bathhouse, whose power was to decide if you deserved a key to a locked cupboard or simply a bamboo basket in which to stow your belongs. Sometimes a novel serves as a mirror; but in other cases it serves as a veil over the meanest reality.

Not all the humor in Fortress Besieged has aged well; I winced, during my recent reading, at some of the jokes targeted at women’s physiques. But only a reader of propaganda, rather than of literature, could denounce the novel on those grounds alone. Much of the book’s abundant comedy could have descended either from the Qing Dynasty satires or from Dickens and Don Quixote. But is humor the point of the novel? I don’t know, and I often wonder how Qian Zhongshu would think of “satire” as a label for Fortress Besieged—one of the few works of fiction he produced in a long and prestigious scholastic career, including being a major translator of Mao Zedong’s work into English.

Advertisement

A work of satire carries laughter and wit in its social criticism, but it also gives readers a buffer. How many of them, after all, want to face down their own flaws and follies? Few Chinese read­ers I know, when laughing at the characters in Fortress Besieged, are laughing at themselves. They are laughing at their in-laws, their bosses, the lovers who have jilted them, and the high-status people they despise but can combat only with mockery. In that sense, satire has its raison d’être in producing a kind of compensation and relief. A satirical novel and its readers meet at a height where, arms inter­twined, they can look down upon some people and some situations with a sense of superiority—more often than not a false one.

There is a character named Bilibin in War and Peace, a Russian diplomat whose forte is to produce mots that then circulate widely in society. He satirizes the French and the Russians and the Austrians and the Germans equally, and neither military nor civilian dignitar­ies escape his verbal lampooning. He will neither win nor lose the war for Russia, but he is a perennial winner in any situation—so long as there is a safe distance between himself and the cannonballs (and there always is that distance for people who know how to play it safe). He is, I often think, the prototype of those witty voices we’ve been hearing on social media for these past twenty years. There is a limit to even the greatest satire, which depends on this sort of safe distance between the satirist and his audience.

I suppose one could call Fortress Besieged a satire, as one could say about Jaroslav Hašek’s The Good Soldier Švejk or some of Isaac Bashevis Singer’s stories, but none of these writers—Hašek or Singer or Qian Zhongshu—was simply a Bilibin. To read them, for all their wit and irony, is to taste a fear or hear an alarm for human beings in crisis. Qian Zhongshu might have been prescient enough, pessimistic enough, or indifferent enough not to pay much attention to how future generations would understand his novel. (In a famous anecdote, he declined a foreign scholar’s visit, saying that a good enough egg should not cause its consumer to want to meet the hen.) But if I read Fortress Besieged as satire thirty years ago, on this rereading I sensed tears when I laughed.
