entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the early hours of Sunday, August 3, 2025, Edward Coristine, a nineteen-year-old computer programmer who had achieved notoriety as an employee of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, was walking a friend back to her car near U Street in Washington, D.C., when they crossed paths with a group of teenagers. According to prosecutors, only one approached at first, demanding the keys to the car. More joined, and some of them punched Coristine, he later told the police, causing him to suffer abrasions, a bloody nose, and head swelling. (He refused medical attention on the scene but subsequently told Fox News’s Jesse Watters that he had a broken nose and a concussion.) Police quickly arrived, and the group fled with Coristine’s iPhone.

By Tuesday President Donald Trump had posted a photo of a blood-streaked Coristine on Truth Social along with a warning that crime in the District was “out of control.” Within days he announced a federal takeover of D.C., using the threat of teenage “thugs” attacking “innocent Citizens” as a pretext for sending in the National Guard—part of a playbook he would subsequently deploy in other Democrat-controlled cities. (A person close to the case disputed the characterization of the teenagers as “some militarized group”—it was “a bunch of kids” that included “innocent bystanders.”) Trump also took the Coristine assault as an occasion to call for another shift: “The Law in D.C. must be changed to prosecute these ‘minors’ as adults, and lock them up for a long time, starting at age 14,” he wrote. Teen offenders “are not afraid of Law Enforcement because they know nothing ever happens to them, but it’s going to happen now!”

Trump’s post fueled calls on the right to try more teenagers accused of crimes as adults. “Young criminals who escape adult criminal court because of their ‘tender’ years should be made responsible for the crimes that they commit,” US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro wrote in a Washington Post op-ed on August 12, 2025. Mocking an event advertised by D.C.’s Department of Youth Rehabilitation Services, she added: “Ice cream socials for hardened repeat offenders just doesn’t cut it.” When the Coristine case resulted in a boy and a girl, both fifteen, being given probation instead of referred to adult court—sentencing in line with what prosecutors had requested, according to the Post—Trump and Pirro pilloried the judge. (Pirro later charged additional members of the group with multiple crimes from that night, including the assault. One teenager incarcerated at eighteen has been held in jail for over ten months without trial, despite having no prior arrests.)

Congress has signaled that it is open to granting Pirro the power to refer more minors for harsher punishment: last September several House Democrats joined with Republicans to pass legislation that would lower the age at which certain youths in D.C. can be tried as adults, from sixteen to fourteen. Her office can already transfer sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds charged with serious crimes to adult court without any judicial review; about a dozen teenagers (all Black) were held in pretrial detention in D.C. under this law as of August. Because of D.C.’s lack of statehood, critics fear the House bill, if enacted, could lead to younger kids being sentenced to facilities contracted with the federal Bureau of Prisons, a system that is ill-equipped to rehabilitate children. It is one of several bills waiting in the wings of the House and Senate that would cause teenagers and young adults to serve longer sentences and acquire criminal records that follow them long after they’re released. Taken together, these pieces of legislation represent not just an attack on D.C.’s self-governance but a broader ideological push to lock up young people rather than prioritize returning them to their communities.

Meanwhile, youth advocates worry that the message coming from Washington could encourage prosecutors to impose these ideas on a case-by-case basis. In New Jersey in April 2025, Trump’s pick for interim US attorney, Alina Habba, announced that she would use a federal law to charge a fourteen-year-old, who was accused of killing one police officer and injuring another, as an adult, since New Jersey state law mandates that people under age fifteen be tried in family court. The state’s then attorney general, a Democrat, also expressed support for changing the state law so that the teenager could be charged. (Habba has since resigned after a federal appeals court found that the Trump administration installed her in her position unlawfully.) “The message is very clear,” Habba told The New York Post. “If you’re a child, I don’t care.”

This attitude suggests a growing backlash against decades of successful advocacy for more humane treatment of young people by the criminal justice system. Starting in 2005, the Supreme Court handed down several decisions that established a framework for treating kids differently from adults, including outlawing the death penalty for juvenile offenders—defined in that case as those who committed a crime while under the age of eighteen. Since the late 2000s, states have increasingly moved away from trying and incarcerating kids as adults in the justice system. Teenagers not considered mature enough to vote, smoke, serve on a jury, or, in some places, drive should not be held culpable for mistakes in the same way as adults, the thinking goes. The number of kids in both juvenile and adult jails and prisons has dropped dramatically over the last two decades.

Advertisement

These shifts were, in part, driven by neuroscience research indicating that adolescents’ still-developing brains respond much better to a rehabilitative justice model than a punitive one, which in turn reduces recidivism. MRI studies have found that the frontal lobes of the brain that are vital to decision-making, including impulse control, are among the last to reach maturity—the process is completed well after the age of eighteen, according to an amicus brief submitted by psychologists to the Supreme Court in 2004. As a result of this period of rapid development, children’s brains may also be more vulnerable to trauma: one 2009 study found that adults who recalled experiencing many adverse events during childhood had life expectancies almost twenty years lower than those of their peers. (Subsequent researchers posited a link between childhood stress and biological changes, since the association with premature mortality persisted even after accounting for socioeconomic and behavioral factors, like smoking.) All of this suggests that incarceration and its harms can have especially long-lasting effects on children.

Such research arrived as incarcerated youth and their supporters—including a coalition of directly impacted Black and brown parents—were already campaigning in courts and the media against juvenile imprisonment, as the journalist Nell Bernstein reported in her 2025 book, In Our Future We Are Free: The Dismantling of the Youth Prison. At the peak of the movement’s success, in 2021, forty-seven states had “Raise the Age” laws on the books, which keep children under eighteen from being automatically sent to the adult system for most offenses. (Vermont, in their law, included eighteen-year-olds and laid the groundwork for some nineteen-year-olds to be included in the future.) “At a moment when regressive forces threaten to stall or unravel progress on multiple fronts, the unlikely success of this movement holds a crucial message,” Bernstein wrote: “transforming an entrenched institution in the service of justice is possible.”

The Covid-19 pandemic jeopardized that progress. At first youth advocates hoped that lockdowns might motivate communities to embrace alternatives to incarceration. In the spring of 2020, as schools across the country shuttered, states faced a choice about whether to also release kids from jails and prisons, where the virus could spread rapidly. In some jurisdictions, authorities decided to isolate incarcerated youth, at great risk to their mental health: Louisiana placed some kids in twenty-four-hour solitary confinement, where they “became so starved for human contact that they dismantled their light fixtures and used the pieces to dig holes in the walls that separated them,” Bernstein reported in her book.

Elsewhere—most notably across California’s already dwindling state system—intake was halted, or kids were released. (Though in California, as Bernstein wrote, they were instead “shunted to county juvenile detention centers that are just as bad or worse.”) There were clear racial disparities, with Black youth less likely to be released than white youth. But the total population in juvenile detention plummeted by almost a quarter in March 2020, according to a survey of agencies in thirty states conducted by the Annie E. Casey Foundation, a private philanthropic organization focused on young people. Arrests also dropped during this time, in part because schools were closed.

Advocates hoped the trend toward decarceration would last. “A lot of us were, I think now, foolishly optimistic,” Marsha Levick, a juvenile law expert, told me. Instead, violent crime, including homicides, temporarily spiked in major cities—a result, researchers at the Brookings Institute suggested in hindsight, of teen boys being out of school and young men out of work in low-income neighborhoods. Politicians on the right seized the opportunity to push a broader narrative about the failure of progressive criminal justice policies. Homicides remained high through 2022, then quickly went back down, trending toward prepandemic levels. But anxieties about crime surged: between 2020 and 2023, the share of Americans who indicated they were afraid to walk home alone at night rose from 29 to 40 percent.

Kids became a particular target of this panic. While the vast majority of people arrested for violent crime in 2022 and 2023 were adults (over 90 percent, according to an analysis of FBI data by the Council on Criminal Justice, a nonpartisan think tank), an entire genre of sensational media story took shape around the temporary uptick in crimes committed by youths. “‘It’s Fight Night’: Disturbing Video Captures Teen Mob Beat Up Off-Duty Firefighter,” read one New York Post headline from 2021. “Disturbing Video Shows Terrified Woman Attacked by Mob During ‘Teen Takeover’ of Downtown Chicago,” read another from Fox News in 2023.      

Advertisement

Carjackings were a special focus. During a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing devoted to the issue in March 2022, the president and CEO of a trade association that works to stop insurance crime painted a picture of juveniles—“some as young as eleven”—stealing cars to commit drive-by shootings. Senators blamed such thefts on the policies implemented in blue states and cities: Marsha Blackburn mentioned Rachael Rollins, then the US attorney for Massachusetts, while Ted Cruz blamed “district attorneys funded in significant part by George Soros” for carjackings and homicides.

These images of teenage mobs taking over cities resurrected a familiar trope. In 1995 the political scientist John J. DiIulio, Jr., then a professor at Princeton, wrote a cover story for The Weekly Standard arguing that the US, and especially Black urban neighborhoods, was incubating a generation of “super-predators” who would bring about a wave of violent crime. “The demographic bulge of the next 10 years will unleash an army of young male predatory street criminals who will make even the leaders of the Bloods and Crips…look tame by comparison,” he warned, predicting that these products of an environment of “moral poverty” would rape and murder without remorse.

This alarmism was itself a reprise of previous moral panics, including the 1970s hysteria over muggings by Black youth in Britain that Stuart Hall and his coauthors famously wrote about in Policing the Crisis (1978). DiIulio’s theory arrived as politicians were already clamoring to be seen as tough on crime, pushing policies such as “three strikes” and “truth-in-sentencing” laws that mandated lengthy prison terms and limited early release. Harsher sentencing—which President Bill Clinton’s 1994 crime bill incentivized—hastened America’s march toward mass incarceration. It also contributed to a feedback loop, in which rising incarceration fed the perception that locking more people up lowered violent crime, when the two trends were not so clearly linked. Trump helped spread this racialized panic, too: in 1989 he took out full-page newspaper ads calling for the return of the death penalty in New York following the arrest of the Central Park Five, a group of Black and Hispanic teenagers—the youngest of whom were fourteen—who were wrongfully convicted of assaulting and raping a white woman. (They were all exonerated in 2002 and later sued Trump for defamation over statements he made about them during a 2024 presidential debate.)

The crime wave DiIulio foresaw never came to pass, and he eventually disavowed his theory. “The superpredator idea was wrong,” he said in a PBS documentary that aired in 2019. “Once it was out there, though, it was out there.” Indeed, it had measurable consequences for Black and brown youth; by the end of the 1990s state legislatures across the country had hardened their approach toward juveniles, as an analysis by The Marshall Project of the propagation of the superpredator myth found. (DiIulio declined to comment for this story, citing health issues.) Starting in 1992, over a dozen states added or changed their laws to establish mandatory minimum sentences for various categories of juvenile crimes. Eleven states lowered the age at which certain juveniles could be transferred to criminal court. Between 1993 and 1995 alone, the average daily population of juveniles held as adults almost doubled nationwide. With kids as young as fourteen coming into the adult system, prisons were struggling with their “new mandate to house them,” observed researchers in a 1996 Justice Department report. Even then, they suggested that many of the legislative changes were based on “public perceptions of the escalation of violent juvenile crime” rather than evidence.

Despite the reformist turn of the later 2000s, the biases reinforced by the superpredator panic persist. A 2014 study found that police officers perceive Black children suspected of felony conduct to be four and a half years older than their actual age, and white children to be almost a year younger. In another study from 2012, white participants were more likely to consider juvenile offenders as blameworthy as adults if they first read that an adolescent who committed a rape was Black as opposed to white.

Such prejudices have clear implications for the way kids are treated by the criminal justice system. A report by the Sentencing Project, a nonprofit that seeks to end mass incarceration, found in 2019 that about half of white children’s delinquency cases were handled informally outside of juvenile court—still a much lower proportion than youth advocates would like—compared to 40 percent of cases involving Black children. And while the percentage of white youths’ cases that judges waived to adult court fell by over 70 percent between 2005 and 2021, the percentage of Black youths’ cases only fell by about 40 percent. In 2023 Black kids were held in juvenile detention facilities at over five times the rate of white ones, according to the Sentencing Project, the highest disparity since tracking began in the late Nineties.

When I interviewed Kristin Henning, a law professor at Georgetown University who works with children accused of delinquency, and who pointed me to such research, she told me that of the several hundred kids she has represented in over a quarter century in practice in D.C., only four have been white. “The superpredator myth,” she said, “lives on in the subconscious of all of us who are making decisions.”

The rhetoric about a teenage crime wave unleashed by Covid-19 was never so neatly borne out by data. Between 2020 and 2023, the country did see an uptick in the number and proportion of juveniles arrested for violent crimes, but the rates, which had been falling for decades beginning in the Nineties, still remained at or below prepandemic levels, according to the Council on Criminal Justice analysis. Juvenile justice experts attributed the increase to a small group of youth struggling—as adults did—with the unprecedented circumstances of the pandemic.

Yet “tough-on-crime” forces blamed the youth for driving an epidemic of violent crime in blue cities. They often traced such violence to progressive policies that in some cases predated the Covid-19 lockdowns. In January 2023 New York City’s then police commissioner, Keechant Sewell, said that the city had seen an increase in the number of juvenile-involved crimes, and pointed her finger at the state’s Raise the Age law, which passed in 2017 and began to go into effect in 2018. Former NYPD Assistant Commissioner Kevin O’Connor told The New York Post that the law had led to fewer kids being arrested and that, therefore, “recidivism is skyrocketing.” Critics often cite a rise in youth shootings after the law’s passage. But a 2023 analysis of New York City police data conducted by researchers at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice found that changes in gun violence among youth “mirrored the scale and direction of trends among adults aged 18 and older.” According to a 2025 report from the NYC mayor’s office, in 2024 felony youth recidivism was about the same as it had been in 2018. “Needless to say, but the debate around criminal justice policies such as [Raise the Age] tends to be heavily agenda driven,” wrote René Ropac, a senior research associate at John Jay, in an email to me.

Even in New York, which has seen a rise in the number of kids arrested for serious violent felonies, the total has remained relatively low: 334 kids in 2024 as compared to 136 kids in 2018. No one wants to see the rates of murder or other serious crimes rise, said Gladys Carrión, a former commissioner for the New York State Office of Children and Family Services. But she questioned why Raise the Age was getting so much attention. “It’s the environment that we’re in now,” she lamented. “After Covid, and this return to being ‘tough on crime’—that really is driving it.”

When it comes to narratives about crime, “kids make an easy target,” said Jeff Asher, an expert in evaluating criminal justice data. Even as violence by kids is rare, the idea that some children are innocent and vulnerable while others are born to inflict harm lends itself to sensationalism. (“The baby-faced suspects…will be treated as adults” for the “grisly killing,” reads one recent New York Post story.) Conflating concerns about the state of the youth with anxieties about violent crime does a disservice to both, said Tom Woods, a senior associate at the Annie E. Casey Foundation. “You’re not really dealing with either one,” he told me.

In addition to the D.C. bill that was passed in the House and still waits in the Senate, two states have overturned part or all of their Raise the Age laws since the start of the pandemic. North Carolina Republicans overrode their Democratic governor in 2024 to revoke part of a bipartisan law from 2019; sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds accused of serious felonies in the state now begin their cases as adults. In 2024 Republicans in Louisiana, which had enacted a Raise the Age law in 2017, reversed it altogether, meaning that the state now prosecutes all seventeen-year-olds as adults.

Asher testified twice in the Louisiana statehouse that rolling back the law was not likely to have any effect on crime rates, because adults commit the vast majority of violent crimes. But he sensed that his data was not convincing lawmakers nearly as much as a presentation by a district attorney, who shared a video of teenagers stealing a gun from an unlocked truck and a music video from YouTube in which Black kids rap while showing off weapons. “Look at them. They’ve got more guns than Kellogg’s got cornflakes,” the DA told lawmakers. He alleged that because seventeen-year-olds don’t have consciences like adults, they “will take you out.” One Republican lawmaker claimed that “some of these kids are already lost when they’re two years old.”

New York has also seen a sustained attack on its Raise the Age law. Last year Jessica Tisch, the current New York City police commissioner, called to change the legislation “before more kids get killed.” Even supporters of the law have questioned its implementation. Money allocated by the legislature to fund county programs for at-risk youth stalled, with almost $1 billion languishing unspent in Albany, as Politico has reported; juvenile facilities were also strained by an influx of older kids. This left the law open to the criticism that alternatives to criminal court don’t work. (Governor Kathy Hochul ultimately protected the law against pressure from district attorneys to roll it back.)                    

Elsewhere, Vermont’s legislature has delayed further rollout of their Raise the Age law, with the state’s Republican governor pushing to repeal it for nineteen-year-olds. Kentucky, Missouri, and Tennessee have all recently eased the path to try teenagers as adults for certain crimes, as The Atlantic reported, as has Mississippi for kids as young as thirteen. Meanwhile, in 2021, the Supreme Court issued a decision that makes it easier for states to sentence juveniles to life without parole. What this effectively means, as The Marshall Project has pointed out, is that in states that haven’t banned such sentences, judges already handing down this punishment will have even more discretion to do so.

From New York to D.C. to Louisiana, attacks on Raise the Age laws reflect the same hardening attitude toward kids accused of crimes. So far, the rhetoric has outpaced actual changes in policy, cautioned Joshua Rovner, a senior research analyst at the Sentencing Project. One reason for hope is that after several years in which polling showed that Americans felt there was more crime in their areas following the pandemic, new Gallup surveys suggest they feel there is much less. And a handful of states have passed progressive laws, such as one that went into effect this month in Minnesota redirecting children under thirteen out of the juvenile justice system altogether. Nonetheless, in addition, “many regressive laws have passed,” Rovner observed.

The treatment of youth offenders, like so much else in US politics, is becoming a site of polarization. Between 2000 and 2025, the proportion of Americans who indicated that violent juvenile offenders should be treated more leniently than adults rose from 24 to 50 percent. Among Republicans, however, the trend has reversed: between 2023 and 2025, the share of Republicans who said juveniles should be treated the same way as adults rose to 65 percent, the highest level in over twenty years.       

The consequences of this attitude can be nightmarish. Over a decade ago, I reported on teenagers who were physically and sexually abused while housed with adult prisoners in Michigan. According to interviews, documents, and videos I obtained, some had been restrained until they urinated on themselves, or gassed with chemical spray; a number had attempted suicide. One testified that a guard threatened to “rape my fat ass if I wasn’t seventeen.” Two others told me directly about being sexually assaulted.

Long after I finished the Michigan story, these horrific episodes would play on repeat in my mind as I tried to sleep. But years later, I also remember the kids themselves. One dreamed of being a deep-sea diver. Another told me about looking forward to caring for the dogs that visited the prison as part of a program for the incarcerated. At the time, across the country, lawmakers of all political persuasions increasingly agreed that locking up children like adults was bad policy. Michigan was an outlier. Following a class-action lawsuit in which the state attorney general’s office sent a representative to follow me into the prisons and subpoena me for my handwritten notes, youth settled with the state of Michigan for $80 million. (The state said that its Department of Corrections “was never able to corroborate the allegations made by plaintiffs about widespread sexual abuse in state prisons.”) Michigan became the last state in the US to end the practice of treating all seventeen-year-olds as adults, in 2019.

As such laws came under fire in the years since the pandemic, the number of kids held in juvenile detention also crept back up. For Black youth, those numbers at one point surpassed prepandemic levels: in January 2020, 1,185 Black youths and 431 white youths were detained across the juvenile detention facilities that the Casey Foundation surveys; by January 2024, the Black population was up 29 percent while the white population was down 4 percent. “At the start of the pandemic, those disparities were pretty large,” said Tom Woods, who tracks this data for the Casey Foundation. “And they have grown since.” This is mostly due to changes in length of stay: nonwhite youth, especially those who are Black, stay in detention longer, Woods noted. As of January, the total detained population had fallen below 2020 levels, but racial disparities persisted.

Children charged in adult court are rarely actually convicted and sentenced to adult prisons, meaning they’re more likely to spend time in a punitive adult jail. But even juvenile facilities can include adult-style punishments like restraints and solitary confinement. According to a recent class-action lawsuit in Colorado, a twelve-year-old diagnosed with autism has been incarcerated in a juvenile detention facility for over six months, despite a judge’s order that he be released. His lawyers report that the boy, who enjoys playing Clue, has been particularly upset by being taken to court in handcuffs. (“We take the concerns raised in the lawsuit very seriously,” wrote a spokesperson for Colorado’s division of youth services.)

In Louisiana, both teenagers whose cases were handled by the juvenile system and those affected by the rollback of the Raise the Age law have reported abuse; the state has also been accused of mixing teens with adult detainees. Teens have alleged being cut off from their families and education: “I am only one credit short of graduating from high school, but there is no school,” one juvenile held in jail in Louisiana testified last year, according to court documents obtained by The Appeal. The teens claim they’ve been confined in modified shipping containers that the jail calls “pods”: “I call the pods slave chambers. The pods are out in the middle of a field next to a jail facility like slave quarters used to be. The guards treat us poorly and they are almost all white. They call us ‘boy’ or ‘boys.’ They are very quick to use mace and put their hands on us.” In 2024 several youths alleged to an investigator that they were also maced inside an adult dorm. They were forced to “crawl up closer to the vents, attempting to find air,” the investigator wrote. The majority of seventeen-year-olds affected by the rollback of the state’s Raise the Age law are accused of nonviolent crimes, and nine out of ten of them are Black, a 2024 ProPublica and Verite News examination of several large Louisiana parishes found. (A spokesperson for Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry’s office did not respond to an emailed request for comment.) 

To advocates for incarcerated youth, simply keeping Raise the Age laws on the books is not enough to prevent the enduring trauma caused by the prison system. For one thing, as Levick pointed out to me, many states still have a far lower minimum age of transfer eligibility, or no minimum at all, meaning younger kids can end up in adult court for especially serious offenses. An eleven-year-old was recently charged as an adult in Pennsylvania for killing his adoptive father; he allegedly found keys to a gun safe while looking for his Nintendo Switch, which had been taken away. 

In a more sympathetic world, we might offer young people different choices and open up the possibility of different lives. In New York City, a coalition of youth justice providers recently argued that community-based organizations should be able to access Raise the Age funds through a competitive process; they imagine using these resources on existing programs that pair young people on probation with mentors from similar backgrounds and offer them paid internships. On the other side of the country, Bernstein reports on youth at the Young Women’s Freedom Center in San Francisco, a nonprofit founded as mass incarceration surged in the early Nineties, who come together to read texts such as Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed. “People who are in survival mode don’t have time and space to reflect, and to problem-pose, and to think critically, so that’s what we do in those circles,” Jessica Nowlan, the organization’s president, told me. (Nowlan herself was one of these young people when she first got involved with the Freedom Center in 1996 as, in her words, a seventh-grade dropout who had been incarcerated seventeen times.) The kids “do understand oppression, systems, control. But they haven’t had space to think about it,” she said.

Bernstein writes that immediate needs are always “front and center” in these discussions. In imagining their own futures, young people are “seeking the things families in wealthy and middle-class neighborhoods take for granted: safe housing, decent schools, accessible health care, fresh food and clean water, jobs and opportunity.” Nowlan, too, emphasized that we already know what young people need to thrive. None of it has changed since the Nineties. But “we need to be very careful right now,” she said, “because people have far less.” And “what’s at stake is people’s lives.”

entries.content:
One afternoon around 1990, as a teenager working my after-school job in an optometrist’s basement office, I was listening to a local college radio station when the DJ, needing a break, decided to play the entire B-side of a record. I had never heard anything like it. Sludgy grooves, wails of unidentifiable wind instruments, and the clatter of an incongruous mandolin and harpsichord drifted in a steamy cloud of artificial reverb. In the middle of it a young man, supported by several backing vocalists, murmured incomprehensibly: “Je suis le Grand Zombie, my yellow belt of choison/Ain’t afraid of no tomcat, fill my brains with poison.”

I was intrigued when the DJ said that the music was by Dr. John, from his 1968 debut album Gris-Gris. I recognized the name from a track on Atlantic Blues: Piano, a double-LP compilation I had bought as part of my efforts to learn to play in that style. But the music I heard on the radio was nothing like those songs. It was pianoless, nearly formless, not the blues but a suggestion of other dark mental states or colors. Where did it come from?

Born Malcolm “Mac” Rebennack in New Orleans, in 1941, to a white family with a deep history in the city, Dr. John led many lives between his precocious musical start in the 1950s and his death in 2019: session musician, petty criminal, addict, funky hitmaker, Muppet model. With his gravelly bayou drawl and his raffish, behatted, bearded stage presence, he became a kind of global ambassador of “New Orleans music,” a phrase that has a specific meaning in a way that cannot be said about “Los Angeles music” or “New York music,” two other cities where Rebennack lived. It means Black music: jazz, blues, R&B, and, more recently, bounce, the city’s local variant of hip-hop. It is music of loose but forceful grooves, laid-back vocal deliveries (like those of the great Lee Dorsey and Betty Harris, to name just two of the city’s best-known R&B singers), pan-Caribbean “Spanish tinge” (to use the Jelly Roll Morton phrase that became a jazz-writing cliché), parade horns, Mardi Gras Indian chants, and, especially, Storyville brothel piano. Even zydeco, which blurs into Cajun music, is from out of town.

Rebennack was involved with this sound on a professional level from an early age. If you believe his deeply sleazy and entertaining 1994 memoir Under a Hoodoo Moon, as a teenager he was gigging as a guitar player at dives all over the South, writing songs, and producing sessions at Cosimo Matassa’s French Quarter studio with a litany of New Orleans legends, from Fats Domino to Huey “Piano” Smith to Allen Toussaint. After Rebennack got one of his fingertips shot off in a post-gig altercation in Jacksonville, Florida, followed by a brief stint in prison, his friend the pianist James Booker taught him the basics of organ playing, which led to a lifetime behind the piano keyboard. Though Rebennack never achieved anything close to Booker’s tonal nuance, formal risk, eclectic references far outside blues, or effusive magnetism on the instrument, he became the world’s most famous representative of New Orleans piano (with, for a short time, the possible exception of another Booker student, Harry Connick Jr.).

By the mid-1960s, like quite a few of his New Orleans studio-rat friends, Rebennack found himself in Hollywood, applying his skills to records by Phil Spector, The Monkees, The Rolling Stones, and Canned Heat, among many others, in what now looks like a golden age for recorded music. As the industry boomed and technological advances gave rise to the multitrack analog studio, which reigned until the digital transformation of the last thirty years, a professional class of session musicians arose alongside it. The producers who kept the tape machines rolling in Los Angeles studios filled their rolodexes with the names of players adaptable, consistent, and efficient enough to meet the demands of whatever show business needed to record in a union-mandated block of studio time.

Rebennack joined the clique of elite LA session musicians in 1964, thanks to his New Orleans friend Harold Battiste, a producer and arranger for Sam Cooke and the founder of the Black collective record label AFO (All For One) Records, which documented New Orleans’s overlapping R&B and jazz scenes. Primed by the success of Sonny and Cher’s “I Got You Babe” (arranged by Battiste—the oboe was his idea), the Atlantic Records offshoot Atco gave Battiste his own sublabel, Progress. His newfound creative control enabled him to ensconce himself with Rebennack and a gaggle of fellow New Orleanians—plus a few LA friends—in the famous Gold Star studio, where they had just enough time to make the thirty-three minutes of music we hear on Gris-Gris.

The album was “almost like a joke,” Battiste recalled in a 2007 interview with the arranger and journalist Richard Niles:

Advertisement

I asked Mac if he had any ideas of what we could do under my Progress Records deal, and he came up with the voodoo thing. He’s a prolific student and he knew about this legendary cat Dr. John, an old voodoo man. So that album was crafted mixing voodoo with the psychedelic thing—a kind of spoof on the West Coast obsession with underground music. Neither of us thought it would be taken seriously.

What started as a spoof became an enduring document of how LA musicians in the late 1960s could use the tools of their industry to create works of striking depth and strangeness. In that era of the music business the lines between working professional, celebrity, and visionary weirdo often depended on little more than the time of day: Glen Campbell, the guy playing guitar behind the Beach Boys or Sammy Davis Jr. on one session, could be singing a Jimmy Webb song that would make him a superstar on the next; Emil Richards could use his truckload of percussion on a generic film score in the morning and then apply it to microtonal experimental blues at night. On Gris-Gris, without playing any piano and with a lot of help, Rebennack created something well beyond the limits of his work-for-hire piano gigs, a gateway between the music industry’s pitiless capitalism and a realm of raw, funky, enigmatic expression. The unstable, ritualistic groove and otherworldly voices on the album’s last track, “I Walk on Guilded Splinters,” the song I heard in that basement thirty-five years ago, have propelled many listeners through that portal.

In Two-Headed Doctor: Listening for Ghosts in Dr. John’s Gris-gris, the eminent British music critic David Toop offers a book-length exploration of the album’s aural pleasures and historical, cultural, and literary implications. At once a chronicle of the record’s making and a critical analysis of its complex sources in folklore, literature, and a range of musical histories, Two-Headed Doctor is itself a kind of a gateway into a realm of musical appreciation that few of us get to occupy. In Toop’s hands Gris-Gris takes on a wider range of meaning than Battiste and Rebennack could have imagined when they rolled into Gold Star one morning and spun up that Hammond organ.

Toop was well situated to succumb to Gris-Gris’s spell. As a teenager in the 1960s he was, like many British people of his generation, caught up in a love affair with African American music, especially blues and R&B. By 1968, when he heard Gris-Gris, he was a regular at the legendary London Roundhouse, where he cemented his echt-Boomer rock-and-roll credentials by seeing early Cream and Pink Floyd performances but also heard the free improvisation ensemble AMM. He was part of the emergence of an aesthetic that embraced rock and roll, the Western classical-rooted work of John Cage and his circle, the free jazz revolution, and all the other auditory wonders flying across the globe on shiny black discs or warbly tapes, from ethnographic and zoological field recordings to raw commercial product churned out by giant corporations, hyperlocal entrepreneurs, and inspired/crackpot amateurs.

Since the 1970s few critics or artists have done more than Toop to advocate for this expansive way of thinking about music and sound. As a musician his work stretches back to New and Rediscovered Musical Instruments, a split 1975 record with the artist Max Eastley for Brian Eno’s Obscure Records label, and to Alterations, the vertiginous improvising group he formed in the late 1970s with Steve Beresford, Terry Day, and Peter Cusak, which at one moment could sound like early Sonic Youth (several years before they existed) and at the next could be a woozy music hall sing-along or a clattering, slapstick toybox explosion.

As a critic, Toop has long been a music nerd’s music nerd. Starting with Rap Attack (1984), considered by many to be the first book about hip-hop, he has demonstrated a rare ability to write about the many meanings and implications of sound, whether or not it fits prevailing definitions of “music.” He is a lover of discographical minutiae; a collector who treasures rare R&B 45s from way outside the Motown/Stax mainstream, faux-exotic records sold in long-closed tiki bar lobbies, samizdat Black nationalist jazz albums, and Detroit techno 12-inches; a researcher who journeyed deep into Brazil’s Amazonas to record Indigenous rituals; and a writer who can explore all of that with the clarity of an ethnomusicologist or with a woozy, J.G. Ballard–like style that blurs fact and fiction.

Rather than investing too much fixed meaning in ideas like authenticity and authorship, Toop’s way of listening involves the drift of musical material across borders and history. He takes more interest in soundscapes than in discrete songs, and foregrounds demiurge figures like club DJs or genre-agnostic record producers over individual composers or performers (though he still attends lovingly to plenty of those, too). These ways of thinking about music may be exemplified by his influential 1995 book Ocean of Sound, which captures a moment when underground ravers, hip-hop auteurs, archive-diggers, newly Internet-charged file downloaders, and other indefatigable experimentalists helped loosen Anglophone rock and roll’s grip on musical culture—and especially music criticism.

Advertisement

In the late 1990s to peruse the records and CDs in a store like Other Music in downtown New York or Amoeba in San Francisco or Honest Jon’s in London—with bins full of forgotten reggae, Ethiopian jazz, Japanese noise, obscure French Ye-Ye, minor Krautrock offshoots, and of course all the multifarious variants of electronic music, from its early practitioners like the French musique concrète composers and Karlheinz Stockhausen to the dizzying varieties of drum and bass, techno, house, and ambient music—was to enter a Toopian zone. When Toop made New and Rediscovered Musical Instruments in 1975, with rare exceptions like AMM’s performance at the Roundhouse, experimental music was something that happened in art schools, classical conservatories, and state-sponsored laboratories like IRCAM in Paris. Today an experimental music festival is more likely to resemble a dance club than a chamber music recital. The people who enacted this shift—musicians, concert curators, label owners, and critics—were reading Ocean of Sound.

Among Toop’s long-standing interests has been the cluster of musical genres that go under the name “exotica.” His 1999 book of that name is a storm of fiction and fact, personal history, criticism, and speculation, all spiraling around Toop’s pursuit of sound and music—live, imaginary, or in that in-between state: constructed, preserved, and sold in recordings. Exotica LPs like Martin Denny’s Quiet Village or Arthur Lyman’s Taboo—with their lurid Pacific Island covers and percussion-heavy arrangements alluding to Latin American, Asian, and African music without a hint of cultural sensitivity—were big sellers in Fifties and Sixties America. A few decades later they lurked deep in the cheap and disreputable corners of used record stores, the easy listening bins, waiting for a new generation of listeners.1

Les Baxter, who exemplified the style on dozens of records like Ritual of the Savage and Jungle Jazz as well as on scores for films like X: The Man With X-Ray Eyes and How To Stuff a Wild Bikini, is a central figure in Exotica. Though to many listeners Baxter was a hack and a schlockmeister, for Toop his work exemplifies how blatantly commercial music built on raw cultural appropriation and fetishism can take on deeper resonance as it finds listeners attuned to its hedonic aura and kaleidoscopic global vulgarity. “As is the case with many musicians whose commercial instincts do daily battle with an innocent need to be regarded as serious, his work was a crucible for unique skills, fabulous inventions and chronic lapses of judgement,” Toop tells us.

Baxter synthesised many exoticas rich in their own troubled histories—Afro-Cuban, Polynesian, South-East Asian, Japanese and Chinese, African, Brazilian, Central and South American, Caribbean—channelling them through a typically cool-school jazz schizophrenia of exquisitely sensitive textural detail undermined or flattened by brashness. The synthesis culminated in a fabricated exotica without boundaries or sovereignty, a place where hybridisation met its final destiny as pure fantasy.

That synthesis flows through Two-Headed Doctor, which concerns the hybridized creation of another Hollywood-based musician known for his “unique skills, fabulous inventions and chronic lapses of judgement.” Toop’s study of Gris-Gris is on one level an effort to clear away the dense fog of self-mythologizing that surrounds the record’s presentation of its creator. “Mac Rebennack” appears nowhere on the album’s cover; instead the album is credited to “Dr. John, the night tripper,” with songwriting credit going to “Dr. John Creaux.” The persona—assumed for the album in jest, according to Battiste—ended up becoming Rebennack’s identity for the rest of his career.

Toop goes to great lengths to document the reality behind Rebennack’s references, reconstructing his actual history, tracking down the sources for his lyrics, fact-checking his statements to the press, and venturing into frequent digressions on the rich history of New Orleans culture and related topics. There was, as it happens, a real Dr. John. According to Toop, Rebennack claimed family connections to a man of that name who is mentioned in “The Last of the Voudoos,” an 1885 Harper’s essay by Lafcadio Hearn. “My great-great-great grandpa Wayne was busted with this guy for runnin’ a voodoo operations [sic] in a whorehouse in 1860,” Rebennack said in an old interview. Toop can’t document this connection, but he does prove that Rebennack’s claims that he adapted songs he learned in voodoo churches are spurious. Many of the lyrics on Gris-Gris were copied from books about New Orleans music so obvious that Toop already had them on his shelf in England in 1968. The words of “I Walk on Guilded Splinters” were copied almost verbatim from a song quoted in the 1946 book Voodoo in New Orleans, by Robert Tallant, with more lines cribbed from the Louisiana Writers’ Project 1945 book Gumbo Ya-Ya.

Toop also gives ample space to the stories of the musicians who, in some cases, played just as important a part in the record’s creation as Rebennack did, if not more: the tambourine player and vocalist Jessie Hill (whose “Ooh Poo Pah Doo” is a classic of New Orleans R&B), the percussionist Richard T. “Didimus” Washington, the backup vocalist Shirley Goodman, the guitar player Ernest McLean. Each of them pulls on another thread in the book’s tapestry of connections and histories. From Harold Battiste’s work with the drummer Ed Blackwell, Toop makes a quick connection to Ornette Coleman, a frequent presence in his books, and to Toop’s ear a major influence on some of the more jazz-like moments on Gris-Gris. Via the ubiquitous LA session woodwind player (and regular Les Baxter collaborator) Plas Johnson, he gets to talk about the rare Condor effect box that transformed some of the instruments on Gris-Gris into mysterious wails.

As Toop’s references accumulate, they map the vast network of cultural currents that he finds running through Gris-Gris. It makes perfect sense to go, over the course of just a few pages, from Sonny and Cher in the 1960s to Cher’s pioneering use of autotune in the late 1990s to how African ritual masks transform the voice of the wearer as well as the face, and from there to Zora Neale Hurston’s research on New Orleans Hoodoo traditions. At the beginning of a chapter called “Inventing New Orleans,” it takes Toop only one paragraph to go from Cosimo Matassa’s studio behind an appliance shop on Rampart Street to Hearn’s early obsessions with “the grotesque, the sensuous and the spectral.”

At the center of this dense weave of interconnected digressions, musical and otherwise, is the question of race and appropriation. Toop has long been preoccupied by, as he puts it here, “how music is created, who owns it, who can speak for it, how it is sold and how it inhabits human feelings, sense of identity, communality and conflict.” Gris-Gris is a particularly vivid case study for this preoccupation. Rebennack was hardly the only white recording artist in the late 1960s “ripping off Black music,” as Margo Jefferson titled her 1973 essay on the subject. Few of his peers, however, went so far as to appropriate a real person’s name and an entire African American religious practice, then repeatedly lie to—or at least misdirect—the press about it.

The Dr. John character was a mask that allowed Rebennack to bring his version of New Orleans culture into the psychedelic 1960s, and it made him a star. “His frequent muddying of the waters that surrounded him amounted to an insurance policy against accusations of appropriation,” Toop writes. “This amounted to a strategy—conscious or unconscious—of legerdemain that allowed him to sell stolen goods to a young, mostly white audience of rock fans and scribes lacking in the knowledge, experience and curiosity to challenge either their provenance or ethical substance.”

And yet even if Rebennack’s identity was “stolen,” to Toop’s ears the music he, Battiste, and their sidepeople recorded in 1968 still evokes the uncanny presence of ancestral forces—the ghosts Toop listens for. “Gris-gris, as a cultural object, and Dr. John as Rebennack’s construct, occupy an uncomfortable place between these two extremes, of deeply embedded traditions on the one hand, and exploitative fantasy on the other,” he writes.

Like an assistant in a Botanica or spiritual mini-market, Rebennack pulls signs and wonders out of the invisible world as if randomly taking poisons, philters and charms down from the shelves…. Every conjurer, sorcerer, medium masker, magician who makes the ancestors go away or doctor of the supernatural must be fluent in the vocabulary and grammar of disorientation. The art of magic is misdirection.

Toop’s research shows us how strongly these tensions between “tradition” and “exploitative fantasy” vibrate in the groove etched into the vinyl of Gris-Gris. Now that omnipresent digital sound flows through all our devices, it’s easy to forget that, not all that long ago, there was a kind of magic in the very fact that music could emerge from a machine. The artists Toop loves, like Rebennack and Battiste and Baxter and Sun Ra, all navigated the complex systems of fact and fiction, money and artistic vision, technical trickery and human virtuosity that defined the midcentury music business. By pulling his own set of cultural charms off the dusty shelves of history, Toop wants to show us how those systems could sometimes produce magic of their own. At the end of Gris-Gris, he writes, “instruments fade away, leaving only the night sounds of shapeshifters, the faintest whisper of ‘guilded splinters,’ an exhalation of breath. It is as if the spectres have taken over.”

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
When the artifacts of an artist’s life are collected as an archive, they change from river to reservoir, their ideas no longer circulating in the artist’s mind but left for others to navigate. Orienting oneself in the archive of a performance artist can be especially fraught because it consists of the ephemera around a performance rather than the performance itself. How do we experience an artwork that existed decades ago for perhaps only an hour or a day?

Tina Girouard left behind reams of material when she died in 2020, at the age of seventy-three. Between 1969 and 1979 she created some thirty choreographed and lightly improvised performances involving movements, rituals, and symbols drawn from everyday domestic tasks and her upbringing in rural Louisiana; she also made installations, textile works, paintings, and more. All the while, she resisted a definitive view of her art. “I learned not to want to hold on, not to concretize a work to the point of killing it,” she told the filmmaker and writer Liza Béar in a 1973 interview in Avalanche magazine. “I don’t want dead art, I want it to be still breathing.”

Some of Girouard’s performance works do live on in recorded form. She was an early user of video, and in 1970 she began a series about methods of transformation couched as self-care. In Maintenance I: Take One—Role Change, she cuts her own hair, treating the camera as a mirror as she changes her appearance; she called the resulting video a “physical broadcast” to the world. Later that decade she integrated video cameras into her live events, creating versions of the performances that, she thought, could “broadcast an image into the universe that reflects the universe back to itself.”

But often all there is to go on in understanding what Girouard’s work might have looked like are notes, drawings, and photographs. For Beached (1978), performed on the Battery Park City landfill, we have her lists of collaborators and objects (a dozen eggs, five hundred pennies), a loose choreography (“MAKE A MAN ON THE SAND/PUT A MAN IN THE NEST OF SAND”), diagrams of the set-up, and photos of the performance itself, which show a large circle divided into quadrants in the sand, ringed by seated performers digging small holes while an audience watches close by, the Twin Towers and other buildings standing in the near distance.

In 2024 the Rivers Institute for Contemporary Art & Thought and the Ogden Museum of Southern Art organized “Tina Girouard: Sign In,” the first comprehensive retrospective of her work. By bringing together performance videos, installations, fabric series, and other diverse material from her archive, the exhibition sought to highlight Girouard’s view of art as a place to mix the public and private and to celebrate the value of habitual actions, everyday objects, and collaborative work. Its title came from Girouard’s contribution, Moving In-Moving Out-Sign-In, to the inaugural show at P.S. 1 Contemporary Art Center in 1976, where she asked anyone who had spent time in her apartment to sign in on a chalkboard.

A recent book of the same name offers a more freewheeling way to explore what Girouard left behind. Tina Girouard: Sign-In contains informative essays by Andrea Andersson, the founding director and chief curator of the Rivers Institute, and several other contributors, among them the critic Aruna D’Souza and the poet and curator Anaïs Duplan. The centerpiece of the volume mimics the ethos of Girouard’s archive and her art, consisting of more than three hundred pages of personal and performance photographs, video stills, notebook pages, contact sheets, exhibition announcements, interviews, and other printed matter produced between 1970 and 1998, all presented without captions; brief descriptions are provided on a separate sheet of paper slipped into the book like a detached list of wall labels.

The book begins with a “glossary of major terms” such as glyphs, memory maps, test patterns, wallpaper, and food—mini-essays that introduce different aspects of Girouard’s work. It ends with a chronology that mixes her artistic achievements with entries from her datebook and “life events” like her marriage to the musician Richard “Dickie” Landry in 1973 and the opening of her first personal bank account in 1974. That same merger of life and art, domestic and communal, permeates her work. She wanted it to be “a preserve, a refuge,” she told Béar. It was a place where “functionless things are given a function as art, and the art functions as an experience.”

Girouard was born in 1946 in DeQuincy, Louisiana, in the area known as Acadiana, a swath of twenty-two parishes between New Orleans and the Texas border. Her father farmed rice, and her mother was a special-education teacher. When she was five, the family moved west to San Antonio, but Girouard felt a bond with Acadiana’s Cajun culture and cuisine for the rest of her life. She attended the University of Southwestern Louisiana, where she met Landry, and graduated with a BFA in 1968.

Advertisement

In 1969 they moved to New York City, renting a two-story apartment in a neglected building in Chinatown, at 10 Chatham Square, with the painter Mary Heilmann. The building provided ample space for both living and making art, and it quickly became a hub of the 1970s Soho art scene, with some forty artists and musicians residing there at different times during the six years Girouard and Landry lived there. Girouard was soon a central figure in a tight-knit community of sculptors, musicians, dancers, painters, and performers that included Keith Sonnier, Gordon Matta-Clark, Philip Glass, Laurie Anderson, Suzanne Harris, and Richard Nonas.

Heilmann described Girouard and Landry as “genius Cajun cooks,” and Girouard’s big pots of gumbo were a regular feature at Chatham Square dinners with friends, which took their cue from community cooking in Cajun country. A photograph in Sign-In shows the aftermath of one of these evenings, the table burdened with dirty dishes and serving platters, bottles, glasses, and cigarette packets. The communal meals fed into Girouard’s work, as did the improvisatory nature of Cajun and “backwater” blues, which she admired because it was “made by a group of people participating equally.”

In one of her earliest performance pieces, Hung House (1970–1971), Girouard constructed an apartment in miniature in a lofty space at 10 Chatham Square, decorating it with objects and furniture left by friends. The walls were pieces of fabric hanging from a second “floor” created by suspending wood platforms from the ceiling. The art historian Pamela M. Lee describes it in Sign-In as a “makeshift architectural structure recalling a children’s playhouse.” The installation remained in place for eight months. Maintenance was also part of the piece: Girouard and other Chatham Square residents periodically lived in, cleaned, and rearranged the space.

In 1971 Girouard participated in “The Brooklyn Bridge Event,” organized by Alanna Heiss on a condemned pier underneath the Manhattan side of the bridge as part of its eighty-eighth anniversary. More than twenty artists performed music, screened films, and created installations from material gleaned from the neglected waterfront. Matta-Clark roasted a pig, serving five hundred pork sandwiches to visitors.

Girouard set up her installation, Swept House, underneath the bridge, near the water’s edge. Rather than clearing the dirt from the area, she made it a primary material, heaping the accumulated dust and detritus into berms that defined the space, which was modeled on her apartment at 10 Chatham Square. She scavenged a couch, rug, and stove from nearby dumps and arranged them in the rooms to create a public version of private hospitality. As she worked, the neighborhood kids thought she was homeless and started bringing her food. They became her performers. One photograph of Swept House shows three boys hanging out in the tidy space, draped across chairs and cushions that surround an area rug. Another shows two boys at the stove while three others sit around a dining table painted onto the ground.

“It’s an achievement,” Girouard told Béar, “to maintain an open life that other people can share and be made to feel at home in.” She called herself an “artist-activist,” and there was, naturally, a political charge to these invocations of daily life. Along with artists like Mierle Laderman Ukeles, whose performances of acts like scrubbing floors and gathering trash turned maintenance work into public art, Girouard made visible the invisible labor in sustaining domestic and civic environments.

Girouard returned periodically to Acadiana to go “a-gathering,” bringing materials such as linoleum, wallpaper, feed sacks, and fabric back to New York, and maintaining a connection with the multicultural agrarian community. As she put it, “I go there to gather myself as well as gather materials.” In 1969 she received a collection of eight three-by-twelve-foot patterned silks from Landry’s mother, who had gotten them from a man named Solomon Matlock, a Palestinian dry-goods salesman and a relative by marriage. Girouard called the fabrics Solomon’s Lot, and she used them in about a dozen performances and installations in the 1970s. Details of some of the floral material are included early in Sign-In, giving the reader a chance to recognize them in different works.

Advertisement

One of these was Air Space Stage (1972), for which Girouard draped four of the silks from the ceiling in an airy canopy at the exhibition and work space 112 Greene Street (now the address of a Stella McCartney store, though the gallery lives on as White Columns in the West Village). Sign-In’s chronology mentions that daily performances were a part of the piece, but there’s no evidence in the book of what Air Space Stage looked like when activated by the performers, and in the recent exhibition the work just billowed quietly overhead. Yet Girouard thought of the fabric as a collaborator that had come, like her, from Louisiana. In her interview with Béar, she described using it in 1973 at a wake for the Louisiana musician Robert Prado, where it provided a way for a group of people—all women—to connect “with a kind of intensity…to each other and to an activity.”

Girouard’s collaborators—both human and material—begat a network in which one person or object was part of something larger than itself. The book’s glossary entry for suspension explains that Girouard believed that lines connecting any two points could make a world. She expressed the connective impulse in a kind of poem she wrote about a work called The Bridge to Louisiana: A Collaboration with Barbara Dilley (1973):

The Bridge connects:

you to me

us to them

me to it

you to it

it to them

you to them

me to them

now to then

here to there

A collective spirit was in the air during those years. In October 1971 a new restaurant opened at 127 Prince Street in Soho. Called Food, it was an artist-run space founded by Carol Goodden and Matta-Clark, with Rachel Lew, Harris, and Girouard (the location now houses a Marc Jacobs store). In its first three years, Food employed about sixty artists, who made up 84 percent of the restaurant’s workers. The aim was to support the artistic community. As Harris put it, “Rather than attacking a system that was already there, we chose to build a world of our own.”

A contact sheet in Sign-In shows the artists of Food demolishing the interior of the previous restaurant in order to make it their own and goofing off atop the rubble in the bed of a truck. In the renovated space, the entire kitchen, including the dishwashing area, could be seen through a Plexiglas window from the dining area. (“We did not want a noisy, water-consuming, electric-consuming dishwasher, we wanted a person, an artist, one that could use a job,” Goodden recalled.) The restaurant’s openness, with large windows looking out onto the street, created a sense of theater, too: prep, cooking, serving, eating, busing all become a kind of performance in service of community nourishment.

The book includes a sample menu, a modest, typed broadside topped with a photo of the crew changing the exterior signage. Lunch offerings were mostly soups and stews: gumbos, chowders, and vegetable options, as well as more exotic fare like “used car stew” and “liver dumpling stew and alka seltzer.” Food’s hours leaned late—until midnight on weekdays, 3 AM on Saturdays, and 11 PM on Sundays (which were reserved for “special guest chef night”)—a schedule that must have suited the artists’ untraditional working hours. Goodden described Food as a “spin-off” of 112 Greene Street—in other words, a site for artmaking. For Girouard, her labor there was art. “That was my work,” she said of the year she dedicated to the restaurant. “All my friends, all of the energy, was poured in there.”

Food was also used as a meeting place by groups like Anarchitecture, a “think tank,” as Girouard called it, that was active in 1973 and 1974. The word had been coined by Matta-Clark to signal a rejection of traditional thinking about buildings and space. Precise understandings of it varied; Girouard told the art historian Mark Wigley that for her the word pointed to “the relationship with living environments,” or what she called “psychological scale.” She thought in particular that the kitchen should be the largest and primary room in the house. In artists’ lofts, she explained, there were no walls, so the kitchen became the entire space: a place for living, eating, dancing, and working.

As the 1970s progressed, the routines of domestic maintenance in Girouard’s earlier work expanded into more metaphysical rituals. Her notebooks reveal her thinking about seasons, the equinox, and phases of the moon. A photograph pasted into a notebook from around 1974 shows a large, leggy spider suspended against the sky, its web nearly invisible; next to it Girouard wrote the phrase “NONPREMEDITATED UNARCHITECTURE.”

In 1977 she created Pinwheel, commissioned by the New Orleans Museum of Art and performed in its colonnaded Beaux-Arts Great Hall, a venue unlike any she had access to in New York. The work was part of a group exhibition, “Five from Louisiana,” which featured sculpture, music, painting, and sound art by nationally recognized natives of the state, for whom it was a kind of homecoming. For Pinwheel Girouard incorporated the Solomon’s Lot fabrics and other objects representing the region, such as palmetto fronds and Spanish moss. In the performance, four performers—or “personas”—construct four conjoined “world images” by overlapping the fabrics to form a central circle. Each quadrant is defined by materials (animal, vegetable, mineral, and other), as well as by time, colors, and gender, recombining the binary genders into four possibilities, like a Punnett square, or like the permutations in The Bridge, in which each aspect is networked to the others. The performers then ceremoniously fill their spaces with a host of corresponding objects, such as a ball, a machete, a snow globe.

Girouard said of her work around this time that she was trying to find “a world view”—a sense that she was part of something bigger than herself and her own time. She wanted this feeling to extend to her performers and audiences. In Pinwheel she created a world big enough to hold Acadiana alongside the rest of her life. Like the homemaking of Swept House, which is the same whether it occurs in a house, out on the street, or in a performative artwork, Pinwheel confirmed for Girouard that rituals and objects could be adapted anywhere. In a notebook she kept in 1979, she wrote, “I go inside a house, I see things, I know what’s going on in each room, the things tell me.”

Girouard participated in a slew of major international exhibitions and festivals in the late 1970s, including Documenta and the Paris Biennale. But the economic transformation of Lower Manhattan made the area less hospitable to working artists, and several of Girouard’s friends left the city. Matta-Clark died in 1978, and the next year a fire destroyed much of Girouard and Landry’s apartment at 10 Chatham Square, after which they moved back to Acadiana. Girouard retired Solomon’s Lot with the performance of Pinwheel and, in the 1980s, began making paintings based on a language of signs and symbols and using textiles and stencils that elaborated on the patterns and objects she had used in earlier works. Pages in Sign-In excerpted from her “Signs and Symbols” notebook (circa 1979) show her transcribing pictographs and glyphs that she attributes to Ojibwa, Egyptian, and East Asian languages. She declares that “OBJECT WRITING preceded all other forms of abstract communication.” The things tell me.

One of my favorite parts of Sign-In is a line that Girouard wrote at the start of her “Reminder” notebook in scrunched capital letters, like a breathless exclamation: “I AM ME AND I AM GOING THIS WAY.” A few pages in, she continues the thought:

Everyone wants to know where they are going. The artists want to say “where it’s at” and where they are going. But no one can know where its at because in knowing there is no longer any going—going on. I know I am going this way…. A good art thing is then and now and who and where and keeps going on. Those things say what’s going on now but they don’t say what. They are what. Now, why do those things say those things? I dont know but I keep going that way.

These meandering lines come as close to being a manifesto as anything I’ve read by Girouard, though that genre is too formal, too rigid for an artist who saw collaboration and the pleasures of experience as essential qualities of her work. They insist without insistence that even as she embraced a degree of the unknown—incorporating improvisation into her performances and relinquishing control of the outcome—her route of artmaking was the right one for her, perhaps especially because its end wasn’t in sight. They enunciate the kind of mysteries that her archive holds: facts but not necessarily answers, a community waiting to be found.

entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

Geoffrey O’Brien is one of those writers who can write about anything: opera, British postwar film, crime fiction, the Third Reich, Grant Wood, Patti Smith, Duke Ellington, Seinfeld. Yet these subjects are often united by a kind of nostalgia—one prompted by pop culture artifacts. His essay from our August 20, 2026, issue, “A Gust from Another World,” is about the Bridey Murphy craze of the 1950s, which was sparked by the account of a young Colorado woman who discovered, under hypnosis, that she was possessed by the spirit of a long-dead Irishwoman. The dubious story (first documented in a book by her hypnotist, then adapted into a movie) helped give rise to a fascination with the unconscious, hypnotists, the afterlife, and mind control. For O’Brien, who remembers the craze from his childhood, it was “a blast from the country of the dead” that cut through a midcentury world “grounded in practicalities, reassured by material things that functioned: fuse boxes, automobile engines, lawn mowers, power drills, reel-to-reel tape recorders.”

O’Brien has written nine books of poetry, a novel, and ten books of nonfiction. He was for many years the editor in chief of the Library of America book series and has been a contributor to The New York Review since 1987. His criticism has also appeared in, among many other publications, Artforum, Harper’s, and The New Republic, and he has written dozens of essays to accompany Criterion Collection editions of movies, including Young Mr. Lincoln, High and Low, The Lady Vanishes, and Moonrise Kingdom. Over a few days in August, we emailed and spoke on the phone about getting into opera, film archives, and Jane Austen.

Lauren Kane: Let’s start at the beginning. Your writing life began with poetry?

Geoffrey O’Brien: I had the good luck to be born into what amounted to a well-stocked library. My parents were largely self-educated after high school, and both were passionate readers. They had a special interest in theater, so the house was full of plays of all eras and countries, and also much else: classic writers in affordable editions (Dumas, Dickens, Keats, Voltaire, Conrad, et al.), books on art, and loads of the detective fiction they loved. I came upon poetry by poking around in these volumes, Fitzgerald’s Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, Poe’s poems, Coleridge’s Rime of the Ancient Mariner, and whatever caught my attention in various old poetry anthologies, for instance The Riverside Book of Verse and Conrad Aiken’s Modern American Poets. I still have many of those old books and go back to them often.

Because theater was such a consuming topic in the house, I associated poetry first of all with speech and performance. Later on free verse forms attracted me by way of the Psalms (King James), Whitman, and translations of Chinese and Japanese poetry, which eventually led to Pound, Williams, Gary Snyder, Frank O’Hara, and others—at which point (in my late teens) I started making my own attempts. I felt I could write a book about that early process of being a reader before being a writer, and published a small volume called Where Did Poetry Come From a few years ago. It does seem you are never done with beginning.

You began writing about opera in the pages of The New York Review. How did that happen?

Without Robert Silvers I probably would never have written a word about opera. He asked me one day if I was interested in reviewing a production of The Rake’s Progress at the Met; I told him I didn’t know the opera, in fact didn’t know much about opera at all, and what little I did know I mostly learned through recordings rather than live performances. He replied simply that in that case I should go out and see some operas. I followed the advice for several years, something made easier by the fact that the more affordable City Opera was still functioning then, and when he came back with another suggestion I felt ready to at least take a stab.

When I was growing up I did hear a great deal about opera from my oldest brother, a precocious musician who never missed a Saturday afternoon Met broadcast and was already studying Wagner orchestrations as a child. (I enjoyed leafing through his copies of Opera News to read the plot summaries and look at the costumes.) He felt I should see an opera at the old Met before it closed, and took me along with him when I was thirteen—the opera in question was Parsifal, maybe not the best starting point. (A few years later Carmen proved more approachable.) Not being a musician, at first I approached opera as drama enhanced to the maximum degree, with language expanded by music and music framed by visible patterns, structures, colors, and fabrics, analogous in its way to bunraku or kabuki. I still feel like a novice. There is always a moment, watching an opera, when it feels like an unknown labyrinth is opening.

You’ve written recently for us about certain periods in film: Fifties Hollywood, postwar British cinema, the singular work of Buster Keaton. How do you conduct research when writing on film history? If you do archival research, what kinds of things do you hope to discover?

The poet Jack Spicer wrote that poems cannot live alone any more than people can. The same goes for movies. The collective process involved in the making of even one film is extended by the electric impact of films placed in juxtaposition. I’m indebted to the film archivists and programmers who make possible those experiences of immersion, whether in a single body of work or a given time and place. In the Sixties, certain directorial retrospectives at the Museum of Modern Art and Dan Talbot’s New Yorker Theater (Hitchcock, Dreyer, Lubitsch, Sternberg, Keaton), as well as Lawrence Alloway’s curated examination of violence in American films at MOMA, or the New Yorker’s genre by genre explorations of Thirties and Forties Hollywood (featuring many films that were then hard to see): all these made a permanent impression. The effect of bringing a host of films together in this way is never predictable; even familiar elements don’t look the same. You cohabit with them, and it’s very much like slipping into a time warp and making direct contact with what is no longer there. The challenge is to stay open and not make hasty judgments.

You write in the Review’s Summer Issue that long after the Bridey Murphy furor had subsided, she remained a postwar “beacon for a culture awash in the uncanny.” What do you think she, and her story, represented to Americans of the time? How does the uncanny persist in our culture today, if at all?

As Alison Winter suggested in her book Memory (2012), the Bridey Murphy story didn’t so much introduce something new as bring into view currents that had long been there. Many people who read Morey Bernstein’s book came forward with accounts of their own paranormal experiences, and in the following decades these moved from the margins ever closer to the center, incorporated into memoirs, fictions, professional practices (channeling, past life therapy, and much more), or evolving belief systems, whether religious or political or an amalgam of both. When I worked for an occult bookselling firm in the 1970s I was overwhelmed by the range of traditions and trends within their compass, but even then could not have foreseen the scope and variety of what has followed. Bridey Murphy was very much a harbinger of what has emerged and continues to emerge, perhaps not as flamboyantly visible as it was in the Sixties and Seventies, but only as far away as a click or two on a laptop.

What books or recent reading projects have been particularly meaningful experiences to you? You mentioned in an earlier conversation reading through Jane Austen—did you arrive at any new insights about her?

Aside from renewed amazement at each of the novels, I discovered in Austen’s so-called juvenilia a treasury of brilliant comic writing, wickedly observant and demonstrating from the start a genius for parody. If Austen had not survived to adulthood, I think these would be recognized as unique achievements. They are as hilarious as anything I have read by more mature writers. By contrast the remarkable fragment The Watsons—a novel she abandoned—describes a social world akin to that of the finished novels, but seen in a much harsher light by a young woman (another Emma) who has been estranged by long absence from her own family and milieu, and is mortified on her return by “unequal Society, and family Discord…. Hard-hearted prosperity, low-minded Conceit, and wrong-headed folly, engrafted on an untoward Disposition,” until, in solitude, “the dissipation of unpleasant ideas which only reading could produce made her thankfully turn to a book.”
